title: The Unequal Economic Consequences of Carbon Pricing
abstract: This paper studies the economic impacts of carbon pricing. Exploiting institutional features of the European carbon market and high-frequency data, I identify carbon policy shocks and trace their dynamic effects. A restrictive carbon policy shock raises energy prices, reduces emissions, spurs green innovation, but decreases economic activity—disproportionately burdening poorer households. Not only are the poor more affected because of their higher energy spending, but they also experience larger income losses. These indirect, general equilibrium effects via income and employment play an important role in the transmission of carbon pricing policies, accounting for about two-thirds of the aggregate consumption response. (JEL E23, E24, O44, Q41, Q54, Q55, Q58)

title: Reproducible Aggregation of Sample-Split Statistics
authors: David M. Ritzwoller, Joseph P. Romano
abstract: Statistical inference is often simplified by sample splitting. This simplification comes at the cost of the introduction of randomness not native to the data. We propose a simple procedure for sequentially aggregating statistics constructed with multiple splits of the same sample. The user specifies a bound and a nominal error rate. If the procedure is implemented twice on the same data, the nominal error rate approximates the chance that the results differ by more than the bound. We illustrate the application of the procedure to several widely applied econometric methods. (JEL C20, C30, C52)

title: The Returns to Government R&D: Evidence from US Appropriations Shocks
abstract: Based on a narrative classification of all significant postwar changes in R&D appropriations for five major federal agencies, we find that an increase in nondefense R&D appropriations leads to increases in various measures of innovative activity and higher business-sector productivity in the long run. We structurally estimate the production function elasticity of nondefense government R&D capital using the SP-IV methodology of Lewis and Mertens (2024) and obtain implied returns of 140 to 210 percent over the postwar period. The estimates indicate that government-funded R&D accounts for one-fifth of business-sector TFP growth since WWII and imply substantial underfunding of nondefense R&D. (JEL D24, E23, H50, O31, O33, O38)

title: Residential Segregation and Unequal Access to Local Public Services in India: Evidence from 1.5 Million Neighborhoods
authors: Sam Asher, Kritarth Jha, Paul Novosad, Anjali Adukia, Brandon Tan
abstract: We study residential segregation and access to public services across 1.5 million urban and rural neighborhoods in India. Muslim and Scheduled Caste segregation in India is high by global standards and only slightly lower than Black-White segregation in the United States. Within cities, public facilities and infrastructure are systematically less available in Muslim and Scheduled Caste neighborhoods. Nearly all regressive allocation is across neighborhoods within cities—at the most informal and least studied form of government. These inequalities are not visible in the aggregate data typically used for research and policy. (JEL H76, J15, O15, O17, O18, R23)

title: Durables and the Marginal Propensity to Spend
abstract: Durables represent a large share of households' marginal propensity to spend (MPX). We develop a quantitative model of spending that takes durables into account and matches a rich set of empirical regularities simultaneously. Scaling the response of nondurables provides a poor approximation of the MPX on durables when it comes to its distribution in the population, its persistence over time, and its cyclicality. As an application, we study how the MPX varies with the size of stimulus checks and find that it declines more slowly compared to a model of purely nondurable spending. (JEL D11, E21, E32, E62, G51)

title: Union Bargaining Power and the Amenity-Wage Trade-Off
abstract: This paper studies how collective bargaining affects wages and amenities. By merging collective bargaining agreements (CBAs) to linked employer-employee data in Brazil, I combine rich contracted amenities with wage information. I implement a difference-in-differences strategy that exploits a court ruling enforcing CBA continuation (i.e., ultra-activity) to estimate the effects of union bargaining power. Strengthening unions raises wages and amenities without reducing employment—increasing retention despite some labor-labor substitution. A revealed-preference approach shows that amenities account for 45 percent of total compensation gains. These findings suggest that collective bargaining can offset monopsony power, but employers retain the right-to-manage workforce composition. (JEL J31, J32, J42, J51, J52, O15)

title: Firm Adaptation in Production Networks: Evidence from Extreme Weather Events in Pakistan
authors: Clare Balboni, Johannes Boehm, Mazhar Waseem
abstract: This paper considers how far private adaptation may reduce future vulnerability to climate risks. Using data on monthly firm-to-firm transactions from Pakistan, we find that flood-affected firms are more likely to relocate to safer ground and shift purchases toward suppliers in less flood-prone regions and reached via less flood-prone roads. The results indicate that firms are imperfectly informed about flood risk and update their beliefs following floods. We quantify aggregate impacts using a spatial model of endogenous production network formation. The findings suggest that firms' learning will shape the economic impact of increasingly frequent climate-related disasters. (JEL D22, L14, O13, O14, Q54, R32)

title: Inequality and Racial Backlash: Evidence from the Reconstruction Era and the Freedmen's Bureau
authors: Eric Chyn, Kareem Haggag, Bryan A. Stuart
abstract: How do majority groups respond to narrowing inequality in racially polarized environments? We study this by examining the Freedmen's Bureau, an agency created after the US Civil War to aid former slaves and launch institutional reform in the South. Using new historical records and an event-study approach, we estimate the bureau's impact on political, social, and economic outcomes. Vote shares for Democrats, the party that previously championed slavery and opposed Black civil rights, initially eroded in bureau counties, but these impacts faded as federal oversight weakened. Racial backlash emerged rapidly and persisted, suggesting White majorities sought to offset Black progress. (JEL D63, D72, J15, N31, N41)

title: The Inflation Attention Threshold and Inflation Surges
abstract: The recent inflation surge brought inflation back on people's minds. I quantify when and how much attention to inflation changes and derive the macroeconomic implications of these attention changes. I estimate an attention threshold at an inflation rate of 4 percent, that attention doubles when inflation exceeds this threshold, and that supply shocks have stronger and more persistent effects on inflation in times of high attention. Developing a model featuring the attention threshold, I show that attention changes offer a joint explanation for inflation surges, inflation's co-movement with inflation expectations, and a long last mile of disinflation. (JEL D84, E12, E31, E43, E52)

title: The Causal Effects of Global Supply Chain Disruptions on Macroeconomic Outcomes: Evidence and Theory
authors: Xiwen Bai, Jesús Fernández-Villaverde, Yiliang Li, Francesco Zanetti
abstract: We study the causal effects of global supply chain disruptions by constructing a new index of real-time port congestion using Automatic Identification System data from container ships and a spatial clustering algorithm. We develop a model with search frictions between producers and retailers that links upstream production slack to downstream supply shortages and captures output and price responses to supply chain shocks. The co-movements of output, prices, spare capacity, and market tightness provide novel identification restrictions. We find that demand and supply shocks drove US disinflation in 2020, while the inflation surge in 2021 was driven mainly by supply chain shocks. (JEL C43, E31, F14, F23, L14, L92)

title: Trade Interdependence in the Modern Global Economy
abstract: Analyzing global trade interdependence requires an approach that incorporates fundamental features of the modern economy: intense trade in intermediates and the changing availability of alternative partners and substitute products. We use theoretical models of structural gravity to construct measures of dyadic dependence that directly incorporate these features. The measures describe (1) how much trade interruptions damage a country’s welfare and (2) how much additional trade it would take from their existing trade partners to compensate. We then show three important findings. First, the new measures differ from traditional measures based on aggregate trade statistics. Second, they show how, contrary to much common wisdom, the world has not marched inexorably toward greater interdependence. Third, we use China’s foreign assistance, as exemplified by the Belt and Road Initiative, to assess the consequences of one major government policy. Chinese assistance has increased partners’ dependence on China, without a reciprocal increase in Chinese dependence.

title: Councils and Indirect Rule in British Africa
authors: JUTTA BOLT, LEIGH GARDNER, JENNIFER KÖHLER, JACK PAINE, JAMES A. ROBINSON
abstract: Did Western colonial rule transform African political institutions? Despite extensive research on indirect rule, we have little systematic evidence about how colonizers’ aims interacted with the structure of indigenous institutions to shape local governance. We explain why colonizers faced incentives to delegate authority to traditionally legitimate institutions, even in historically decentralized areas. Empirically, we analyze originally compiled data on African political institutions in the precolonial and colonial periods for more than 450 subnational units across British Africa. We focus on councils as a form of executive constraints. Subnational councils were widespread, exhibited strong correlations with precolonial institutions and patterns of socioeconomic development, and exerted meaningful decision-making powers. These indirect-rule institutions reflected reforms to replace ineffective installed agents. Pressure from below prompted British officials to reintroduce systems of executive constraints based on precolonial models. Our findings reject widespread claims that colonizers could unilaterally implement indirect-rule institutions while disregarding precolonial precedents.

title: When Business Speaks, Legislators Listen: Experimental and Qualitative Evidence from Brazil
abstract: The influence of interest groups on policy making is a central concern in representative democracies, yet identifying causal effects remains a significant challenge. This article argues that legislators respond to informational cues about the economic importance and coalition breadth of interest groups. A field experiment in Brazil, which randomized the receipt of printed and WhatsApp messages from a pro-reform business organization, reveals that legislators are more likely to vote in favor of the group’s position when its membership size, economic importance, and sectoral reach are emphasized. A survey experiment with lobbyists supports this mechanism, showing that messages highlighting group characteristics increase legislators’ expected engagement and support. In-depth interviews with key political figures—including a former president, ministers, and deputies—further corroborate these findings. This study contributes to the literature on informational lobbying and cue-based persuasion by employing realistic experimental treatments and mixed-methods evidence.

title: Who Benefits from Citizenship? Varying Effects of Naturalization Decisions in the Early-Twentieth-Century United States
authors: Peter Catron, Nathan I. Hoffmann, Mingze Li
abstract: Citizenship acquisition is widely viewed as a mechanism for improving economic outcomes, yet little is known about whether its benefits are distributed evenly. This article examines the varied returns to naturalization in the early-twentieth-century United States, assessing whether naturalization uniformly benefits all immigrants or is especially impactful for those already positioned to profit. Using naturalization records from New York City’s Southern District in the early 1900s, we construct a novel historical dataset for 1,947 immigrants who declared their intent to naturalize. By linking these records to U.S. census data from 1920, 1930, and 1940, we are able to observe immigrants’ characteristics at the point when they make naturalization decisions and to track their outcomes over time. Our findings reveal that immigrants who completed the naturalization process attained significantly higher occupational status than those who initiated but did not complete naturalization. In addition, citizenship is most transformative for those facing the greatest disadvantages. Additional analyses corroborate these findings in linked full-count census data for the entire United States. Citizenship confers occupational advantages not only through formal rights but as a resource that enables claims-making in the labor market, with greater returns to less advantaged immigrants.

title: Youth Representation and Democratic Legitimacy
authors: Aksel Sundström, Charles T. McClean, Daniel Stockemer
abstract: How does the age composition of democratic institutions shape public evaluations of their legitimacy? While most institutions are dominated by older politicians, we argue that incorporating younger representatives can enhance perceptions of legitimacy. To test this claim, we conduct a survey experiment in the United States that varies the age composition of a bipartisan state legislative committee and its decisions. We find that including younger members increases perceptions of procedural fairness and institutional trust, and improves evaluations of decisions on lower-salience policies. These effects are stronger among young people and Democrats. Evidence on mechanisms suggests these legitimacy gains reflect beliefs that younger politicians are more attuned to young people’s experiences and concerns. Observational evidence from US state legislatures and a replication experiment in the United Kingdom yield consistent patterns, suggesting that these findings extend beyond the original experimental context. This suggests that expanding youth representation can meaningfully strengthen democratic legitimacy.

title: When Can Political Parties Credibly Change Their Policies?
abstract: When can a party credibly change its policy on an issue? No institution forces parties to keep their promises after being elected. Voters may thus view platform shifts as mere pandering, discounting their credibility. We propose that voters use the direction of a platform shift as a signal of the party’s motives and policy commitment. Shifting to an unpopular position is a costly signal of principled motives, while moving toward a popular one suggests opportunistic ones. Two preregistered survey experiments, one evaluating a general setting and another focusing on a real case of mainstream party accommodation to the radical right, show that voters infer party motives and commitment from platform shifts in line with the predictions of our argument. Our study provides important insights into the electoral persistence of radical right parties, party system stability, and why platform shifts often fail to affect voter perceptions of party positions.

title: Power from the People: How Autocrats Use Referendums to Generate Support for Controversial Policies
abstract: Why do autocrats put their initiatives to a public vote? Scholars have only recently turned their attention to authoritarian referendums as a “nominally democratic institution.” Focusing on “voluntary referendums”—cases when rulers hold a public vote despite not being constitutionally required to do so—we advance two claims: first, that autocrats sometimes stage public votes to proclaim nominal popular approval for controversial policies; and second, that organizing such votes can help generate support for these initiatives. We argue that authoritarian referendums are more than discrete voting moments. Instead, they are complex institutions with important upstream components that rulers can exploit. We illustrate this argument using evidence from the Russian 2020 public vote on constitutional amendments, while also showing its applicability across other autocracies.

title: The cultural origins of the demographic transition in France
abstract: This research shows that secularization accounts for the early fertility decline in France. Why the demographic transition began in France a century before any other country is one of the big questions of history because it challenges traditional explanations and because of data limitations. Using a novel dataset crowdsourced from online genealogies, I comprehensively document the decline and its timing. Then, I document the loss of influence of the Catholic Church and find a strong and robust association with the timing of the transition. Finally, I explore the drivers of secularization and discuss the transition’s impact on economic growth.

title: The Effect of Reducing Welfare Access on Employment, Health, and Children’s Long-Run Outcomes
authors: Jeffrey Hicks, Gaëlle Simard-Duplain, David A Green, William Warburton
abstract: Welfare caseloads in North America halved following reforms in the 1990s and 2000s. We study how this shift affected families by linking Canadian welfare records to tax returns, medical care, educational attainment, and criminal charges. We find substantial and heterogeneous employment responses that increased average income despite reduced transfers. We find zero effects on aggregate healthcare costs, but mothers saw reduced preventative care and increased mental health treatment, consistent with the transition to employment elevating time pressure and stress. We find no effect on teenagers’ education or criminal charges as young adults but find some evidence of intergenerational welfare transmission.

title: Local Crime and Prosocial Behaviours: Evidence from Charitable Donations
authors: Carlo Perroni, Kimberley Scharf, Sarah Smith, Oleksandr Talavera, Linh Vi
abstract: We study the relationship between local crime and residents’ charitable donations and explore the mechanisms underlying this relationship. The analysis combines longitudinal postcode-level data on charitable donations made through a UK giving portal with publicly available data on local crime and neighbourhood characteristics. Our main results suggest that an increase in local crime corresponds to a significant rise in the size of unscheduled charitable donations. This pattern is primarily driven by the donation choices of female and gender-unclassified donors. The strength of the relationship between local crime and donation amounts also varies with postcode-specific population characteristics, such as religiosity, age, and mental health.

title: Hezbollah’s Communication Strategy: Emotional Appeals for Cohesion and Resistance
authors: Stephanie Dornschneider-Elkink, Sofia Quaglia, Luke Horton
abstract: While research has traditionally linked resistance to negative emotions like anger and frustration, a growing body of work now emphasises the importance of positive emotions such as trust and hope. This article analyses Hezbollah’s speeches from 2001 to 2023, focusing on anger and trust while incorporating positive and negative affect. Using quantitative methods to detect emotions and affect in natural language, our findings reveal that positive affect – often overlooked in resistance studies – is expressed most frequently, followed by trust, negativity and anger. Positivity and trust appear in discussions of Hezbollah’s in-group and ideology (Islam), while negativity and anger surface in discourse on violent resistance and regional security. These findings challenge Western media portrayals that associate Hezbollah with hate and negativity, suggesting that Hezbollah uses positivity and trust to reinforce cohesion, while leveraging negativity and anger to rally support for resistance activities.

title: Ballots over Barrels: Oil, Democracy and Conflict in Guyana
abstract: The political resource curse posits that newly resource-rich states risk experiencing authoritarianism and conflict. This article examines Guyana as a most-likely case of that phenomenon. Drawing on interviews and quantitative indicators, we find that oil has not driven the recent democratic backsliding and rising geopolitical tensions. Instead, Guyana’s democratic fragility stems from winner-take-all electoral institutions in a context of deep ethnic polarisation and major parties’ limited normative commitment to democracy. Regarding conflict, Venezuela’s domestic politics, not oil, is the key driver of regional tensions. We therefore argue that the political resource curse framework may at times obscure more than it reveals, misattributing long-standing political tensions to resource wealth. Domestic and international political dynamics may be better understood as ‘politics with resources’ than politics cursed by oil. Promoting electoral reform, fostering stronger commitment to democratic norms within political parties and ensuring credible deterrence may therefore matter more than technocratic resource governance.

title: African Youth and the Future of Democracy: How Social Media and Cohort Size Shape Political Participation
abstract: Despite their demographic size and growing political influence, African youth remain understudied in research on political participation. This article examines how two structural shifts, youth cohort size and social media use, independently and jointly shape electoral and protest behaviour across 40 African countries. Using Afrobarometer data (2016–2023) and complementary contextual datasets, we find that individual socio-economic factors remain the strongest predictors of participation, but demographic structure and digital engagement also matter. Larger youth cohorts are associated with a greater likelihood of voting. Social media use is connected with increases in protest participation while reducing the likelihood of voting, and its interaction with youth cohort size shapes both behaviours in important, non-linear ways. These findings challenge assumptions that youthful populations inherently drive unrest and show that digital mobilisation is strongly conditioned by the demographic context. Our study has significant implications for democratic legitimacy and youth inclusion in Africa’s rapidly changing political environments.

title: Navigating Social Sustainability in Refugee Camps Through Transect Walks
abstract: This paper provides a comparative study of the Zaatari and Azraq refugee camps in Jordan, examining how current planning of the built form, layout and design influences social sustainability indicators within the camps. The aim is to examine and identify key socio‐spatial factors that either support or undermine social sustainability in both camps using transect walks. Generally, results suggest that the macro‐scale, characterized by low camp homogeneity and a chaotic path system, was associated with higher fear of crime and lower perception of safety, but was perceived to support higher access to services, amenities and facilities. At the meso‐scale, the urban form corresponds with weaker community networking and social interactions but facilitates social participation and community engagement. At the micro‐scale, characterized by larger shelter areas resulting from appropriation schemes, it promotes a higher sense of pride and place attachment and supports higher levels of everyday agency and a sense of permanence. The findings aim to inform architects, urban planners and inter‐governmental agencies on how spatial strategies can promote social sustainability in the context of planned refugee camps, advocating a comprehensive approach that creates empowering living environments for refugees.

title: After Zombies Attack: How Low-Quality Monitors Affect Credible International Election Observers
authors: Sarah Sunn Bush, Christina Cottiero, Lauren Prather
abstract: The international election monitoring regime has become considerably more complex in the twenty-first century. Although the number of organizations engaged in high-quality election monitoring has plateaued over time, the number of low-quality monitors that validate autocratic elections has continued to grow. This study investigates how low-quality international election observers affect the behavior of high-quality observers when they are present at the same elections. On the one hand, the presence of low-quality international observers may encourage high-quality groups to step up their game, becoming more thorough and (when merited) more critical in a bid to differentiate themselves from low-quality groups. On the other hand, the presence of low-quality observers may discourage high-quality groups from criticizing flawed elections by introducing counter-narratives, accusing high-quality monitors of bias, and challenging the dominance of high-quality monitors. We test these hypotheses using new data on international election observation from 2000 to 2020, finding evidence that high-quality monitors have become more thorough but less critical in the presence of low-quality monitors.

title: Subsystems, Bargaining Costs, and Economic Coercion: The Incidental Consequences of US-Led Sanctions Against Russian Oil Exports
abstract: How do markets affect the distribution of coercive bargaining costs in economic sanctions? This paper uses subsystem theory to study sanctions as market governance arrangements. It argues that sanctions do not rely on coercion alone, but must also provide benefits to market participants. A sanctions sender is unlikely to enforce sanctions that could disrupt markets on which both sender and friendly third-party states depend. The paper further argues that sanctions can create unforeseen problems in other areas of the world economy, but that states tolerate such negative effects to preserve important market benefits. These arguments are illustrated through an in-depth case study of the 2022 price cap on Russia’s oil exports. The United States and its allies did not enforce the price cap strictly, worrying that doing so could disrupt Russian oil supplies and drive up crude prices. They also tolerated significant maritime safety and environmental risks arising from Russia’s price cap evasion efforts—especially its use of substandard “shadow fleet” tankers—to protect global oil markets. Scholars of economic coercion need to pay closer attention to how market arrangements shape the design and implementation of sanctions—and to their incidental consequences in other areas of governance.

title: Assessing Populist Belligerence: Evidence of Populism and Democratic Governance’s Interaction on Interstate Violence
authors: Ariel Zellman, Daniel F Wajner, Carmela Lutmar, Özgür Özdamar
abstract: A burgeoning literature seeks to explain populism’s influence on international security. Two regime characteristics appear particularly troubling in this regard: their degree of populism and their degree of democratic governance. While considerable research has explored these paired phenomena regarding states’ domestic agendas, little work has systematically examined these trends vis-à-vis states’ propensity for interstate violence using large-N quantitative analysis. Drawing on populism data from the V-Dem Party dataset (1970–2014), we examine how these factors contribute to states’ likelihood of threatening or utilizing military force. We find that populism’s effects on interstate bellicosity are particularly pronounced among more authoritarian regimes, however populism increases the likelihood of threat-making and use of military force by democracies and non-democracies alike. Overall, bellicose behavior is less apparent from examining degrees of populism or authoritarianism in isolation than from their interaction. These findings contribute to lively debates on populism’s imprint on international peace and stability.

title: The Price of Incompetence: Security Failures and Selective Accountability in Autocracies
authors: Austin S. Matthews, Jonas Willibald Schmid
abstract: Do dictators hold their cabinet ministers accountable for policy failures, and do such failures push them to appoint more competent replacements? Existing research emphasizes loyalty as the dominant logic of authoritarian elite management, yet many cabinet portfolios carry responsibilities critical to regime survival. We argue that interior ministers, who oversee internal security and counter-terrorism, offer a revealing test of whether performance matters when the stakes are highest. Using an original dataset of more than 1,000 interior ministers across autocracies from 1970 to 2014, we show that deadly terrorism significantly increases the likelihood of ministerial dismissal. Yet, these crises do not lead dictators to appoint successors whose backgrounds signal greater security expertise. The result is a pattern of selective accountability: dictators punish visible failure but do not invest in preventing its recurrence. This asymmetry helps explain why authoritarian regimes often struggle to build effective security apparatuses despite acute survival pressures.

Designing school choice for diversity in the San Francisco Unified School District
authors: Irene Lo, Katherine Mentzer, Mobin YahyazadehJeloudar, Henry O’Connell, Joseph Monardo, Itai Ashlagi
abstract: More than 65 years after the Brown v. Board of Education ruling that school segregation is unconstitutional, public schools across the United States are again experiencing rising segregation. In districts like San Francisco, efforts to implement district-wide choice policies have largely failed to reverse these trends. Since 2019, we have collaborated with the San Francisco Unified School District to design a student assignment policy meeting the district’s goals of diversity, predictability, and proximity. We use optimization techniques to develop policies restricting choice to zones. We compare these to district-wide choice policies by estimating a choice model using historical application data and simulating assignment. Our results show multiple policies can reduce school segregation while preserving varying degrees of proximity, choice, and predictability. Zone-based policies with reserves reduce the concentration of racial minority students in high-poverty schools and maintain proximity, but reduce choice. District-wide choice with reserves and distance-based priority can further reduce segregation, but at the cost of predictability. Tradeoffs are necessary as no policy dominates another policy. In addition, we show that spatial segregation indices capture average patterns in these tradeoffs but miss important variation revealed by our simulation framework. Our work informed the design and approval of a zone-based policy in San Francisco in 2020, and supports ongoing policy implementation.

title: A causal account of the neural origins of mental fatigue
authors: Hongmei Xia, Gizem Vural, Antonia Susnjar, Helge J. Zöllner, Rebekka S. Mattes, Alexander Soutschek
abstract: Successful goal-directed behavior often requires the exertion of effortful cognitive control processes, but it remains unclear why engaging in cognitive control is experienced as effortful and induces fatigue. Here, we tested the hypothesis that sustained activation in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC)—a neural substrate of cognitive control—causally induces motivational fatigue via the accumulation of prefrontal glutamate metabolites. For this purpose, we combined brain stimulation with spectroscopy imaging to assess how increasing DLPFC excitability during an effortful mental task changes the motivation for mental effort and glutamate concentrations. We found that stimulating the DLPFC during mental effort exertion improved mental performance at the cost of increased posteffort motivational fatigue, suggesting a causal role of DLPFC activation for inducing fatigue. On the neural level, DLPFC activation during effortful cognition also increased prefrontal concentrations of glutamate, which statistically explained the fatigue-induced lower motivation for mental effort. A corresponding analysis of combined glutamate–glutamine (Glx) concentrations revealed converging effects. Together, these findings provide causal evidence that enhanced DLPFC activation contributes to fatigue via neurochemical changes, supporting neuro-metabolic accounts of fatigue and offering new insights into why demanding cognitive tasks are perceived as effortful.

title: Lifetime stressor exposure is associated with altered trust formation and social learning in dynamic interactions
authors: Jonas P. Nitschke, Nace Mikus, Livia Scanferla, George M. Slavich, Claus Lamm
abstract: Although trust is fundamental to social interactions, how lifetime stressor exposure relates to the cognitive processes underlying trust remains poorly understood. Using the Stress and Adversity Inventory (STRAIN) to assess cumulative lifetime stressor exposure, combined with an adaptation of the repeated trust game and computational modeling (Hierarchical Gaussian Filtering), we investigated how stressors experienced over the life course relate to three core aspects of trust dynamics—initial trust formation, learning about others’ intentions, and adaptation to changes in trustworthiness—in 168 adults. Greater lifetime stress was associated with stronger negativity biases, lower initial trust, and heightened uncertainty about others’ intentions, increases that were general rather than specific to partner type. These more pessimistic priors were not accompanied by poorer reading of partners: Higher lifetime stress was associated with greater differentiation between prosocial and selfish trustees, driven by reduced investment in the selfish trustee alone. Computational analyses further indicated greater belief volatility, consistent with faster model-implied updating of perceived trustworthiness. These findings provide novel evidence that lifetime stress is associated with a profile consistent with recalibration, rather than a degradation, of the cognitive mechanisms underlying trust, with potential consequences for relationship formation and social functioning. They also provide a computationally grounded framework for understanding associations between adversity and social cognition and generate testable predictions for future experimental work.

title: Epigenetic aging during the COVID-19 pandemic: A prospective longitudinal study with prepandemic baseline data in children, adolescents, and adults
authors: Alicia M. Schowe, Mirko Ruks, Charlotte K. L. Disselkamp, Dmitry V. Kuznetsov, Jana Instinske, Theresa Rohm, Andreas J. Forstner, Markus M. Nöthen, Bastian Mönkediek, Christian Kandler, Darina Czamara, Elisabeth B. Binder
abstract: Psychosocial stress is a risk factor for aging-related diseases. The COVID-19 pandemic placed a psychosocial burden on individuals, potentially increasing the risk for aging-related diseases for which epigenetic clocks are used as early biomarkers. Based on four epigenetic clocks (DunedinPACE, GrimAge2, Horvath, and PedBE), we investigated whether epigenetic aging changed during the pandemic and whether these changes were associated with objective and subjective pandemic-related stressors and preexisting individual risk factors for poorer physical and mental health. We used prospective longitudinal data (n = 1,028), including repeated salivary DNA collection from children (n = 359, MAGE = 9.5 y), adolescents (n = 385, MAGE = 15.5 y), and adults (n = 284, MAGE = 24.3 y). Saliva was collected before the first phase of containment measures in Germany in March 2020 and after the second phase in 2021. We observed significant increases in epigenetic age acceleration (PedBE: b = 0.17, P < 0.0001; GrimAge2: b = 0.08, P < 0.0001) and pace of aging (DunedinPACE: b = 0.13, P < 0.0001) across all age groups. Prepandemic physical health and parental socioeconomic status, but not objective pandemic stressors, were significantly associated with this change. In adolescents, higher perceived pandemic burden was associated with a larger increase in pace of aging (DunedinPACE: b = 0.04, P = 0.01). Together, these findings suggest that prepandemic individual risk factors for poorer physical and mental health are accompanied by measurable increases in epigenetic aging during the COVID-19 pandemic, with adolescence representing a sensitive phase to its psychosocial burden.

title: How 20th-century immigrants did not have to change their last names in order to become American
abstract: Reports of parents’ names in Social Security Application records allow us to quantify at a population level the extent and nature of historical last name changes by immigrants. Our analysis of European, Middle Eastern, and Asian immigrants of the early to mid-20th-century finds that more than 80% kept their last names. Computational linguistic analysis shows that most of those who did change preserved their surname’s ethnic signal, leaving only about 5% of all immigrants trying to disguise their foreign origins. Of these, Jewish immigrants had the highest rate of ethnicity-concealing last name changes; Italian, Japanese, and Chinese immigrants all had the lowest. Our proposed framework helps understand the variation: name changes were rarest where ethnic community networks were densest and where passing as unmarked was least credible—as among visibly non-White immigrants. Our findings challenge the dominant assimilationist narrative that immigrants in this era had to shed their foreign identities to enter the American mainstream. “Becoming White” by adopting an English surname was not a large part of historical immigrant experience. Rather, the overwhelming majority of immigrants chose to openly preserve their ethnic origins. Our results also suggest that nominal record linkage of historical immigrant populations may be more feasible than previously assumed.

title: Unpacking transatlantic income inequality
authors: James P. abstract: This paper uses newly harmonized survey and register data on incomes and labor market outcomes as the basis for consistent comparisons of inequalities across 17 North American and European countries over the period 1995–2021. We examine trends in disposable income inequality in the working-age population, defined as persons aged 25 to 60, as well as its component parts of market income inequality and redistribution through government tax and transfer systems. We adjust incomes to allow for changes in education, population aging, and household structure in each country. We test for convergence across countries in demographically-adjusted disposable income inequality, along with market income inequality and redistribution. There is strong evidence of convergence over time in disposable income inequality across the 17 countries, despite a divergence in the dispersion of market income inequality driven by very heterogeneous trends for hours of work and the number of workers in households across countries. Consistent with this we find a strong convergence across countries in the dispersion of our measure of redistribution. There are reductions over time in inequality-reducing redistribution in the Nordic countries and increases in some other European and North American countries, with the net effect being more similarity across countries, a lower average level of redistribution, and a higher average level of disposable income inequality. These trends are being driven by the bottom 95% of the income distribution. Our results are robust to a variety of alternative specifications including the measure of inequality, trimming of data outliers, and sample period.

title: Patterns of implicit and explicit attitudes V: Increases in bias from 2021 to 2025
authors: Tessa E. S. Charlesworth, Meriel C. Doyle, Mahzarin R. Banaji
abstract: Between 2007 and 2020, implicit and explicit intergroup attitudes declined in bias steadily and were forecasted to continue toward attitude neutrality. But, since 2020, 5 y of new data (2021–2025) from 2.8 million U.S. respondents reveal that past trends have stalled or, in some cases, even reversed. The largest reversals in bias emerged for sexuality, transgender, race, and skin-tone bias which increased by 12 to 22% on implicit measures and by 24% to more than tripling on explicit measures. Age, disability, and body weight bias also increased, but at relatively slower rates. Breakpoint analyses showed that implicit attitudes were early indicators of change, reversing trend ~1 y earlier than explicit reports. For most topics, reversals were widespread across demographic groups and even extended to an international sample of 274,884 non-U.S. respondents. However, younger respondents (<20-y-old)—who had previously shown the largest decreases in bias—now showed the largest increases in bias; these trends also interacted with politics and gender (e.g., young conservative men were the most likely to increase). Exploratory analyses ruled out various single-cause explanations. Instead, we suggest that the best explanation is that 2020–2021 marked a turning point in the sociopolitical climate, whereby co-occurring existential threats from the COVID-19 pandemic, amplified economic insecurity, political sectarianism, and online toxicity prompted increases in intergroup bias. These data underscore how large populations of individual-level attitudes are continually shaped and altered by macro, societal-level events.

title: Trust as a hidden driver of epidemic-relevant behavior: Institution- and behavior-specific associations across 20 national survey waves
authors: Alexander J. Zapf, George Dewey, Katherine Ognyanova, Matthew A. Baum, William P. Hanage, Marc Lipsitch, Ata A. Uslu, James N. Druckman, Roy H. Perlis, David Lazer, Mauricio Santillana
abstract: Compartmental models of infectious disease transmission make assumptions about human behaviors. Specifically, they parameterize interactions across population groups, assumed to have distinct epidemiologically relevant behavioral patterns, primarily through contact matrices stratified by demographic variables such as age, gender, or socioeconomic status. Although such demographic characteristics are readily measurable, they may inadequately capture the social and psychological forces that govern protective behaviors. Drawing on 20 waves of a national survey conducted throughout the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States, we show that institutional trust—particularly trust in public health agencies, physicians, and hospitals—is a dominant predictor of protective behavior adoption. For mask wearing during periods of strongest pandemic activity, institutional trust explains more behavioral difference across population groups than age, income, education, and partisan affiliation combined. In unadjusted analyses, the difference in protective behavior adoption between individuals with the highest and lowest trust in the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) was four- to six-fold larger than the corresponding differences by age, income, or education, and exceeded the difference between Democratic and Republican respondents. This association was institutionally specific (the relationship attenuates for trust in banks), and behaviorally specific (trust in the CDC is associated with protective behaviors but not visiting a doctor). The latter suggests that trust modifies voluntary compliance with public health recommendations rather than healthcare access or use. These findings identify institutional trust as a candidate stratifying variable for models of behavior-coupled transmission dynamics, and as a measurable target for public health surveillance.

title: In-group neural alignment serves as a biomarker of social identity
authors: Yohay Zvi, Nitai Kerem, Eldad Aviv, Yaara Yeshurun
abstract: In this study, we propose a perspective on neural synchronization. Beyond reflecting shared understanding between individuals, we suggest it serves as a biological marker of social homogeneity. We examined fMRI neural responses of 42 participants (21 religious, 21 secular) watching neutral and religion-relevant video narratives. While explicit measures of emotional response, agreement, and engagement showed no significant differences in within-group variance, religious participants—representing a tighter social structure—exhibited significantly higher in-group neural synchrony across all content types and brain networks. Remarkably, synchrony values predicted religious orientation with an accuracy of up to 92%. We conclude that a community’s homogeneous social structure drives pervasive neural alignment, positioning neural synchrony as a potential signature of group cohesion beyond explicit behavioral measures.

When do citizens support government decisions to ignore social protests? The role of instrumental considerations and majoritarian preferences
abstract: In democracies, protests can challenge public policy reforms, raising questions on how governments should respond. Our study examines how citizens in the Netherlands would prefer their governments to respond to social protests. Using a pre-registered survey experiment (N = 1262), we varied the level of government implementing a reform and the level of public support for a reform. We used observational data to assess respondents’ views on the reforms and their trust in the government. While our findings reveal relatively strong support for accommodating social protests, citizens are more likely to back governments that ignore protests when these reforms have majority support and align with their own views. Trust in the government also plays a role, but the level of government does not matter for citizens’ attitudes. Overall, our findings highlight that citizens expect governments to listen to social protests but their attitudes are further contingent upon instrumental reasoning and majoritarian views of democracy.

title: Digging Into the Subsoil: Considering and Theorizing Human Services Delivery at the Sub‐Micro‐Level of the Public Service Ecosystem
abstract: Public services are often delivered in partnership with families and communities, yet these relationships receive limited attention within public service ecosystem (PSE) theory. Responding to call to develop the sub‐micro‐level of the PSE, we introduce the concept of subsoil sensitivity to foreground the family and community ecosystems that underpin public service value creation. These informal systems are active sites of value creation and destruction with sensitivities arising from their alignment or misalignment with public services. We propose legislative and policy nodes as connectors that translate macrolevel policy into microlevel practice. Drawing on child protection vignettes, we show how nodes create the conditions for interaction, while subsoil dynamics influence whether value is cocreated or codestroyed amid power asymmetries and differing belief systems. The paper extends the sub‐micro‐level of the PSE and offers a framework for examining family and community ecosystems in public service delivery.

title: Cult of Personality or Lack of Competition? Determining Trump’s Sway Over Republican Partisans on a Critical Case
abstract: It is well established that partisans follow their leaders. While this potentially has important implications for political accountability, studies of opinion leadership rarely examine accountability directly. We test whether partisans are able to hold a dominant leader accountable under favorable conditions using a critical case: Trump’s position on the Epstein files. Two preregistered experiments, fielded before the release of the Epstein files, show that partisans follow Trump and do not hold him accountable when he is unopposed or contested by the Democrats. However, when Trump faces opposition from within his own bloc—especially countermessaging from right-coded media elites—both issue-specific and overall approval decline substantially, and following is halved. Our results have two important implications. First, opinion leadership does not imply the absence of political accountability. Second, meaningful political competition in polarized societies may need to originate from within ideological blocs. While Trump is powerful, credible opposition can make him accountable.

title: The Effects of School Phone Bans: National Evidence from Lockable Pouches
authors: Hunt Allcott, Jason Baron, Thomas Dee, Angela L Duckworth, Matthew Gentzkow, Brian Jacob
abstract: Schools across the U.S. have sharply restricted student use of phones during the school day. We evaluate one type of restriction—lockable phone pouches—using nationwide data combining a large-scale teacher survey, GPS pings, standardized test scores, and school administrative records, along with sales records from the largest pouch provider. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design, we find that pouch adoption substantially reduces phone use as measured by GPS pings and teacher reports. In the first year after adoption, disciplinary incidents increase, and we find suggestive evidence that student subjective well-being falls, consistent with short-term disruption. However, disciplinary effects fade, while the estimated effects on well-being appear to recover and become positive in later years. For academic achievement, average effects on test scores are consistently close to zero. High schools see modest positive effects, particularly in math, while middle schools see small negative effects. We find little evidence of effects on school attendance and no clear evidence of improvements in self-reported classroom attention or perceived online bullying.

title: Why Do Union Jobs Pay More? New Evidence from Matched Employer-Employee Data
authors: Pierre-Loup Beauregard, Thomas Lemieux, Derek Messacar, Raffaele Saggio
abstract: We use Canadian matched employer-employee data to assess the sources of the union pay premium. After controlling for worker heterogeneity using the two-way fixed effects approach of Abowd, Kramarz, and Margolis (AKM), we find that unionized firms pay about 15 log points more than non-unionized firms. Forty percent of this gap is linked to productivity differences between unionized and non-unionized firms as measured by value added per worker. The remaining gap reflects unions’ ability to extract more rents for workers. Our estimates imply that unions raise pay among unionized workers by around 9 log points, with considerable heterogeneity by industry and firm birth cohorts. The union effect grows to about 11 log points in an extension of the AKM approach where unions also affect the returns to unobservable worker characteristics.

title: A Model of Enclosures: Coordination, Conflict, and Efficiency in the Transformation of Land Property Rights
abstract: Economists and historians have long debated how open-access areas, frontier regions, and customary landholding regimes transformed into private property. This paper analyses decentralized enclosure processes using the theory of aggregative games, examining how population density, enclosure costs, potential productivity gains, and local governance capacity, including the power to demand compensation, jointly determine the mix of property regimes. Depending on these fundamentals, private decisions to enclose may be strategic complements or substitutes. Strategic complements generate tipping points and socially destructive property races, whereas strategic substitutes produce smoother transitions and may leave enclosure below the social optimum. While policies to strengthen customary governance or compensate displaced stakeholders can realign incentives, addressing one distortion while neglecting others can worsen welfare.

title: The first 1000 days: Modeling language learning from individual children’s everyday speech
authors: Hadas Raviv, Arkadii Tsyhanov, Kira Gousios, Aja Altenhof, Haocheng Wang, Berlin Chen, Ofri Raviv, Tal Rosenwein, Casey Lew-Williams, Liat Hasenfratz, Uri Hasson
abstract: Children learn to understand and speak from the speech around them, yet how that everyday input shapes learning remains unresolved. Large language models show that language is learnable from data, but their scale and training conditions differ sharply from a child’s natural experience. We trained cognitively feasible, child-specific models on longitudinal home recordings from eight children across their first 1000 days of life. Each model learned incrementally from a single child’s ordered speech input without prior linguistic knowledge, developing phoneme-like and word-form representations that tracked each child’s learning pace. Learning was dependent on dense daily sampling and replay of recent input, indicating that both experience- and memory-related processes are necessary. These findings show that everyday experience contains sufficient structure for language learning and establish child-specific modeling for testing developmental theories.

title: Denoising the US Census: Succinct block hierarchical regression
authors: Badih Ghazi, Pritish Kamath, Ravi Kumar, Pasin Manurangsi, Adam Sealfon*
abstract: The 2020 United States Census adopted differential privacy to protect individual confidentiality, adding calibrated noise to summary demographic measurements that are then reconciled into population tables. We developed BlueDown, a postprocessing algorithm that combines techniques from linear regression and constrained optimization while exploiting measurement structure for efficiency. On 2020 Census data, BlueDown reduced the error of groupings by race at the county level by 21 to 36% and of all county-level groupings by 9 to 58%; at the tract level, it reduced error of groupings by housing type by 38 to 61%. These gains came at no cost to confidentiality or computational efficiency and would improve the validity of research relying on this definitive dataset and analyses used to guide the distribution of more than $1.5 trillion in annual federal spending.

title: Music divisions and cultural hierarchy in China: how transnational, political, and historical forces shape symbolic boundaries
abstract: This study maps the division of music in China and examines the mechanisms underlying its formation. Methodologically, it introduces multidimensional item response theory (MIRT), a latent-trait approach rarely used in cultural sociology, to identify the social divisions of taste before examining their social stratification through regression analysis. The findings reveal six taste profiles: high-status traditional music; pop music stratified into middlebrow Hong Kong and Taiwan classics, unstratified mainstream Chinese pop, and low-status local music; and foreign music divided into high-status selective forms and unstratified trendy foreign pop. These divisions do not cleanly align with genre categories, a highbrow–lowbrow hierarchy, or omnivore–univore patterns in established accounts. Instead, they reveal dual forms of high-status taste—state-consecrated heritage and cosmopolitan selective foreign pop—reflecting a multidimensional structure organized around region of origin, historical prestige, cohort, and popularity. More broadly, this study reveals how cultural stratification in China extends beyond Bourdieusian models centered on domestic field competition to encompass global flows, state-directed legitimation, and historical local trajectories. These findings extend theories of cultural distinction beyond the assumptions derived from dominant Western liberal-market societies and offer a framework for understanding how cultural hierarchies are constituted across wider national contexts.

title: Workplace authority in China: gender, parenthood, and work sectors
abstract: Workplace authority is a key individual and organizational resource to which women typically have more limited access than men. Yet, less is known about how parenthood shapes this gender disparity and how the relationship varies across employment regimes. Drawing on nationally representative, longitudinal data from the China Family Panel Studies (2010–2022), I examine within-person changes in women’s and men’s access to supervisory authority following parenthood, with particular attention to variation across the state and private sectors. Fixed-effects results show that, overall, women’s likelihood of holding authority declines after becoming mothers, especially after having two or more children, whereas men experience little change. These dynamics differ by work sector. A considerable motherhood penalty is concentrated in the private sector, whereas a fatherhood premium emerges only in the state sector. Parenthood therefore widens the gender gap in authority in both sectors through distinct patterns. These findings suggest that employment regimes condition the gendered meanings of parenthood and how they translate into access to authority. In China, the state sector’s formal protections may buffer motherhood-related disadvantages, whereas its male-dominated hierarchy and pronatalist agendas may sustain fatherhood-related rewards.

authors: Anne Solaz, Eija Lindroos, Carole Bonnet, Mia Hakovirta, Daniel R. Meyer, Milla Salin
abstract: Highlights Joint physical custody remains strongly stratified by education, even in European countries where JPC is widespread. Medium-educated parents catch up with highly educated parents where JPC prevalence is high. Low-educated parents remain less likely to use JPC, regardless of its prevalence across countries. JPC use with young children remains lower, even in countries where shared care is widespread. Flexible forms of JPC (unequal share) are more common in low-prevalence countries.

authors: Nicolás Soler, Tom Emery, Agnieszka Kanas
abstract: Highlights Register data enable researchers to study support availability in country-wide family networks. Survey data can be linked to the register networks to study actual support. Network structure is associated with self-reported availability of family support. Family networks extensively overlap because relatives are present in multiple families.

title: Parental Separation and the Quality of Ties to Extended Kin
abstract: Highlights Parental separation involves reorganization at all levels of the family system. Young adults who experienced parental separation have weaker ties to extended kin. These ties are especially weaker on the paternal side. The gaps are smaller in cases of joint physical custody after parental separation.

title: Transforming Manhood: Women's Employment and Other Sociodemographic Predictors of Testosterone in American Men
abstract: Highlights This investigation of the predictors of testosterone in American men focuses on the integration of women in the labor market. Men's exposure to women in the workplace is inversely associated with testosterone levels. Other variables significantly predict testosterone, for example, age, race and ethnicity, and marriage. Our results shed light on population-level declines in testosterone worldwide.

title: Evidence on the Robustness of the Links Between Social Relationships and Mortality
authors: Rosanne Freak-Poli, Stephen P. Jenkins, Michael A. Shields, Trong-Anh Trinh
abstract: Highlights New evidence is provided on the robust links between social relationships and mortality. Analysis uses 19 waves of Australian longitudinal data for individuals aged 50+. Functional and structural social relationships each independently predict mortality. Loneliness is most strongly associated with a higher mortality risk. Investing in social relationships would help protect against mortality risks.

title: Marriage and Premarital Cohabitation Timing for LGB Adults in the United States: A Research Note
authors: Jessica Noblitt, Miles G. Taylor, Wendy D. Manning, Claire Kamp-Dush
abstract: Highlights Gay and lesbian adults cohabit longer before marriage and marry at older ages than heterosexual adults. Bisexual women in same-sex relationships marry nearly six years later and cohabit about 1.5 years longer before marriage than bisexual women in different-sex relationships, who marry younger than any other group. Age at cohabitation varies little across groups, and differences by partner sex among bisexual men are not statistically significant.

title: The Short-Term Fertility Impact of Abortion Law Restrictions: A Research Note
authors: Anna Matysiak, Lucas van der Velde
abstract: Highlights Poland's 2020 abortion ruling led to a sharp 6% drop in births 37 weeks later. The decline exceeded the number of legal abortions previously performed. The decline was strongest among younger and childless women. Abortion bans may reduce fertility when they heighten risks of childbearing.

title: Trends and Patterns in Childlessness by Age, Race and Ethnicity, and Education in the United States: A Research Note
authors: Benjamin-Samuel Schlüter, Leslie Root, Monica Alexander
abstract: Highlights We present a Bayesian parametric model to estimate the percentage of childless U.S. women across age. There have been substantial changes to childbearing trajectories for women born in 1950–1999. The share of women who are childless has increased across most ages in younger cohorts. This increase has not yet had substantial effects on the share of women without children at age 45. Young cohorts would need to experience significant rises in births in the 30s to match earlier cohorts’ low childlessness at age 45.

title: The Invention of Liberalism
abstract: Today, it is commonplace to claim that liberalism created the modern world. This paper examines how and why the rise-of-liberalism narrative first emerged by examining textbooks and surveys on the history of political thought published in Britain and the United States between 1890 and the 1990s. In doing so, it shows how, in the interwar period, a new conception of “liberalism” was invented, imagining it as a secular emancipatory movement that shaped the modern world in its image. Second, this paper highlights how this master narrative was created by liberalism’s self-professed enemies—by Marxists and conservative thinkers—as much as by its friends, to serve different polemical purposes. Finally, this paper offers some reflections on the implications of this account of the historiography of liberalism for its contemporary defenders. It concludes that liberals themselves might have good reason to relinquish overblown claims about the importance of liberalism in the making of the modern world.

title: Women and the double standard of ambition
abstract: Few human qualities are as morally unstable as ambition: We seem unable to decide whether to admire or condemn the desire for self‐advancement. This instability guarantees double standards—and none has been more enduring than that of women's ambition. This article traces the emergence of this double standard in early modern England, when ambition came to be widely accepted as natural and even virtuous in men, yet remained unnatural and vicious in women. It then turns to four seventeenth‐century feminists—Rachel Speght, Margaret Cavendish, Mary Astell, and Judith Drake—who challenged this emerging double standard. They reimagined ambition as a feminist tool, using it to argue for women's equality and even superiority. Unearthing this neglected strand of ambitious feminism not only contributes to the history of political thought but also points the way to a reconciliation between feminism and ambition that avoids the pitfalls identified by feminist theorists today.

title: Can citizen election observation increase public confidence in US elections?
authors: Jennie Barker, Oren Samet, Susan D. Hyde
abstract: Nonpartisan citizen election observation plays an important role in promoting the credibility of electoral processes around the world. This article assesses whether nonpartisan observation can shape attitudes among the US public, randomizing information about nonpartisan domestic observers in a series of survey experiments fielded to nearly 10,000 respondents. These included both hypothetical vignettes and information about a real‐world nonpartisan domestic observation mission undertaken by The Carter Center during the 2022 midterm elections in Fulton County, Georgia. The results show that information about positive assessments by nonpartisan observers of the hypothetical and Fulton County elections increased respondents' confidence in electoral results and processes, and also made respondents more likely to identify the officially announced winner over the candidate they favored as the candidate who won. Alternative ways of framing observers were largely inconsequential.

title: Capturing Demographic Burden Over Time with the Cumulative Dependency Ratio
authors: Guillaume Marois, Wolfgang Lutz, Klaus Prettner
abstract: The age dependency ratio is widely used to summarize population structure and to inform discussions of economic potential and population aging. However, as a period measure, it reflects the demographic balance at a single point in time and is highly sensitive to the timing of fertility and mortality change. This paper introduces the cumulative dependency ratio, a longitudinal reinterpretation of the traditional indicator that aggregates person‐years lived in dependent and support ages over a specified horizon. By explicitly incorporating the temporal dimension, the cumulative dependency ratio provides a person‐year‐based summary of demographic burden and facilitates comparison across periods, regions, and demographic scenarios. Using examples for the United States alongside comparative analyses across world regions, the paper illustrates how a cumulative perspective smooths short‐term demographic fluctuations, reduces sensitivity to the choice of observation year, and reframes the relationship between population structure and long‐run economic performance. Viewed through this cumulative framework, future fertility changes primarily affect the timing of dependency rather than its cumulative magnitude, and long‐run differences in demographic burden across regions appear smaller than implied by period measures. The cumulative dependency ratio complements existing indicators by providing an interpretable summary of sustained demographic pressures and intergenerational balance.
