Partisan social cognition and biased experiences in a polarized world: The neural processing of identity‐based group membership
authors: Adam Moore, Sujin Hong, Cyril R. Pernet, Alexa M. Morcom, Neil Roberts, Agamemnon Krasoulis, Laura Cram
abstract: Pairing neuroimaging and behavioral testing, we offer new insights into affective polarization, hyper‐partisanship, and their effects. Our findings introduce a temporal dimension to existing theoretical frameworks concerning the impact of social identity on political perceptions. We demonstrate that group‐identity shapes in‐the‐moment neural processing of real‐world experiences in a functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) protocol and Cyberball game where participants experience varying levels of inclusion/exclusion from in/out‐group members. In other words, people don't simply rely upon group membership (e.g., partisanship, national identity) to post‐hoc rationalize an experience, but instead that group membership also actively biases neural processing of otherwise objectively identical experiences, shaping (and distorting) political perception, with significant behavioral effects.

title: The rhythm of persuasion: Media channels, psychological priming, and voting decisions through political music in Nigeria
authors: Ukamaka C. M. Ozioko, Success Esomchi Obi, Anibueze U. Anselm, Agaba Joseph David, Chinasa Emelda Nnanyelugo, Charles Chukwudi Eze, Jude Chukwudi Agbo, Gever Verlumun Celestine
abstract: The objective of this study was to determine the effect of exposure to political music on voting decisions among Nigerian voters. Data were collected from a multistage sample of 388 participants, and logistic and linear regression models were applied to evaluate the hypotheses. The findings revealed that an individual's overall exposure to political music significantly predicts their likelihood of voting, demonstrating a small positive effect size (Odds Ratio = 1.08). Rather than operating through indirect moderation pathways, exposure media and geographic location emerged as the strongest direct predictors of persuasive influence. Specifically, direct exposure via local radio ( β = .21) and shared audio files ( β = .12) significantly predicted a voter's influence score. Furthermore, rural voters reported being significantly more influenced by political music than their urban counterparts, with geographic location operating as the strongest overall direct baseline predictor ( β = −.48). The study concludes that the psychological effectiveness of political music lies not in generalized, blanket exposure, but in a targeted strategic focus that leverages specific media channels and subcultural demographic segments to maximize persuasive impact on voter behavior.

title: The critical role of political trust in the energy transition
authors: Jordana W. Composto, Sofía Silvosa, Anandita Sabherwal, Elke U. Weber
abstract: Achieving net‐zero CO 2 emissions requires sustained collaboration between civil society and the private and public sectors across time and geographies, but low trust in and among these actors impedes coordinated action. This multidisciplinary review examines how different forms of trust, in particular political trust (i.e., trust between actors with differential power), shape the energy transition, addressing four core questions: How does trust impact energy project development and outcomes? How do the processes of building, maintaining, eroding, and repairing trust differ? What are the asymmetries in trust gain and loss? How does a project's history and stage determine which process is at play and whether trust repair is possible? A narrative literature review and analysis of fifteen case studies spanning diverse energy contexts identifies key trust dyads: government‐community, developer‐community, regulator‐developer. Mapping these trust dyads on project outcomes reveals when trust functions as either a barrier or a pathway to success. We complement our literature review and case analysis with primary data from stakeholder surveys and expert workshops that validate the real‐world relevance of trust research insights and identify the largest trust deficits and effective trust‐building strategies perceived by expert practitioners. Our findings across sources of evidence converge to show that political trust operates through distinct mechanisms across different actor relationships, with direct implications for project design, stakeholder engagement, and policy implementation. The review concludes by outlining future research directions and opportunities for cross‐disciplinary collaboration to address trust challenges in the energy transition.

title: Unrequited: Zero‐sum asymmetry in the political domain fuels affective polarization
abstract: Zero‐sum beliefs about political relationships—the conviction that one party's gains are inevitably offset by another party's losses—have often been cited as drivers of partisan conflicts. However, across five studies with diverse samples of U.S. residents ( n = 1383), four of which were preregistered, we find that overall zero‐sum endorsement shows weak and inconsistent associations with affective polarization. Instead, beliefs are frequently one‐sided: Many individuals endorse the idea that their political opponents' gains are harmful while rejecting the notion that their own gains come at others' expense. We refer to the strength of this outgroup‐ingroup imbalance as zero‐sum asymmetry . Across correlational and experimental studies, higher zero‐sum asymmetry reliably predicts heightened partisan animosity. At the same time, it is associated with higher civic efficacy and, in several samples, greater political participation and democratic commitment. Notably, symmetric zero‐sum endorsement is relatively rare compared to asymmetric patterns. Together, these findings highlight the directional structure of perceived political trade‐offs as a key contributor to affective polarization, with broader implications for how citizens interpret partisan competition and evaluate the health of democratic systems.

title: Beyond remembrance: Genocide commemoration as a lens for understanding collective victimhood and contemporary conflicts
authors: Mengyao Li, Ani Grigoryan, Slieman Halabi, Anna Baumert
abstract: Genocide commemorations are a key societal mechanism through which collective victimhood is constructed and transmitted across generations, yet their implications for contemporary conflicts remain underexamined. We conducted parallel naturalistic longitudinal studies in Armenia around Armenian Genocide Remembrance Day and Israel around Holocaust Remembrance Day (Time 1), with a lower‐salience comparison 2 months later (Time 2). Across both studies, Armenian and Jewish‐Israeli participants reported heightened existential threat and reduced inclusive victim consciousness around Remembrance Day than at the post‐Remembrance Day assessment. Armenian participants also reported lower willingness to reconcile with Azerbaijan, while their attitudes toward Ukrainian victims of the Russia–Ukraine war did not differ significantly across time. In Israel, attitudes toward the conflict with Palestinians did not differ significantly across time, but participants reported greater willingness to help Ukrainian victims at Time 1. Time 1 indirect effect analyses further revealed competing pathways: greater personal involvement in commemoration was indirectly associated with more conflict‐supportive attitudes (via heightened threat, moral entitlement, and reduced inclusive victimhood) and with more conciliatory and prosocial attitudes (via heightened moral obligation). These findings highlight that genocide commemorations are linked to competing psychological processes, which may explain their divergent implications for intergroup relations, a tension discussed in the paper.

title: Distinction Without a Difference: American Public Opinion on Immigrants and Refugees
abstract: Do Americans hold refugees in higher regard than immigrants? If so, why? We theorize that refugees activate humanitarian concerns and perceptions of deservingness, while immigrants trigger threat perceptions and competition, leading to divergent mental associations toward each group. We investigate these questions with a nationally representative online survey experiment fielded in 2024 that contrasts Americans’ attitudes toward refugees and immigrants using both open- and close-ended questions. Open-ended mentions reveal that refugees trigger themes of involuntariness, conflict, and humanitarianism, while immigrants elicit themes of domestic politics, fairness, and threat. Close-ended responses indicate that Americans view immigrants as more competent and more agentic than refugees, and they associate refugees and immigrants with different reasons for coming to the United States. Despite these differences in beliefs, respondents report no significant differences on warmth stereotypes, group affect, or policy preferences. Thus, while Americans do possess some divergent beliefs about refugees and immigrants, ultimately these are distinctions without a difference when it comes to group affect and policy opinions.

title: Correction: A Healthy Democracy? Evidence of Unequal Representation Across Health Status
Bridging the Migration-Climate Divide: Toward Climate (Im-)Mobility Research 3.0
authors: Andréas Litsegård, Karsten Paerregaard, Ibrahim Wahab, Elizabeth Carper, Gyanu Maskey, Truphena Mukuna, Deliang Chen, Julia Curio, Xiaoye Yang, Anders Burman
abstract: Over the past decade, a growing body of empirical and theoretical research has examined the relationship between climate change and human (im-)mobility. Yet this literature remains fragmented geographically, methodologically, and theoretically, particularly in how it conceptualizes and integrates the multiple drivers shaping mobility outcomes. Despite growing recognition of the multicausal nature of climate-related (im-)mobility, few studies have developed genuinely integrative interdisciplinary approaches that bridge climate research and the social sciences. This article addresses this gap by advancing a research agenda capable of analyzing how climatic and non-climatic drivers interact to shape people's livelihoods and decisions to move or stay in a changing climate. Its contribution is twofold. First, it critically reviews existing analytical frameworks to assess how they conceptualize interactions among mobility drivers, their relationship to climate change, and the ways in which climate change reshapes mobility dynamics. Second, building on this review, it advances an interdisciplinary climate (im-)mobility research agenda 3.0 that gives equal analytical attention to mobility and immobility and integrates natural and social science perspectives, methods, and data. As a first step towards operationalizing this agenda, the article proposes a novel application of Factors Constellation Analysis (FCA), an approach originally developed in health sciences. Adapted to climate (im-)mobility research, FCA provides a flexible analytical framework for systematic examination of how various constellations of climatic, environmental, demographic, social, cultural, political, and economic factors interact to produce different (im-)mobility outcomes.

title: Humanitarian Migrants’ Non-Metropolitan Settlement and Subsequent Internal Migration
authors: Cho Yat Wong, Aude Bernard, Tomasz Zając, Charles Siriban, Jing Wu, Francisco Perales
abstract: To accommodate the influx of humanitarian migrants and address rural depopulation, many countries promote non-metropolitan settlement amongst incoming humanitarian migrants. Yet many humanitarian migrants subsequently leave their initial non-metropolitan settlement locations, which raises questions about the effectiveness of non-metropolitan settlement policies and the factors influencing humanitarian migrants’ relocation decisions. Within this context, this research note leverages Australian population-level administrative data from the Person Level Integrated Data Asset (PLIDA) to generate novel insights. Specifically, we analyse aggregate data comprising 3.4 million annual bilateral internal migration flows between 87 local labour markets for humanitarian migrants from different origin countries over the 2011–2019 period, comparing their patterns to those for the general Australian population and other migrant groups. Our findings indicate that non-metropolitan areas experience net losses of humanitarian migrants to metropolitan areas, and that humanitarian migrants relocate to regions with greater employment opportunities, better education options, and larger co-ethnic networks. Importantly, the patterns and determinants of internal migration for humanitarian migrants often differ to those observed for other migrant groups as humanitarian migrants are less responsive to labour- and housing-market conditions, but more responsive to co-ethnic networks. Altogether, our results highlight the difficulty of stimulating non-metropolitan population growth via humanitarian migration, with implications for other receiving countries.

title: Learning democracy: The lasting effects of political education on democratic support
authors: Anja Neundorf, Roman-Gabriel Olar, Johannes Gerschewski, Rosalind Shorrocks, Natasha Lindstaedt
abstract: Do citizens need to grow up in a democracy to value it? We examine how school education – democratic or authoritarian – shapes long-term support for democracy. Leveraging a quasi-natural experiment in the former German Democratic Republic, where rigid school entry rules and abrupt reforms after reunification created exogenous variation in exposure to socialist schooling, we show that an additional year of such education significantly reduced democratic support in adulthood. To test generalizability, we analyze harmonized survey data from 106 countries alongside new expert-coded measures of educational content and state effort. The results reveal that democratic attitudes are shaped not only by the negative imprint of authoritarian schooling but crucially by the positive imprint of democratic civic education, especially when democracies invest heavily in it. Our findings demonstrate that democracy must be learned to be valued, underscoring the central role of education in democratic consolidation and resilience.

title: ‘We sleep with the head inside, but the brain outside’: local integration in resettlement’s shadow
authors: Manya Oriel Kagan, Maria Nagawa, Noa Rubinstein
abstract: How do refugees perceive resettlement policy, and how do these perceptions influence local integration outcomes? In this article, we argue that refugees experience UNHCR’s three durable solutions—integration, resettlement, and repatriation—as interdependent rather than separate pathways. We investigate our argument in Uganda, drawing on in-depth qualitative data from twenty key informant interviews and five focus group discussions with thirty-four participants conducted in Kampala and two refugee settlements. Our findings reveal that refugees navigate resettlement and local integration policy domains concurrently and that their perceptions of one solution shape their engagement with others. Moreover, even though refugees cannot apply for resettlement, they proactively pursue resettlement and make decisions they believe might help their cases. This dynamic is fueled by an information environment where unclear eligibility criteria and limited transparency result in a reliance on informal information networks. The findings not only highlight the costs of siloing refugee protection solutions but also demonstrate how refugees proactively navigate policy spaces.

title: Unsettling Integration: Decolonial Acts of Belonging. Edited by Fiona Murphy and Ulrike M. Vieten
The Immortality Paradox: One‐Party Dominance, Political Tenure, and Organizational Continuity in Japanese Agencies
abstract: In his classic 1976 study on organizational survival, Kaufman argued that public organizations are “immortal”. More recent research, however, has come to the opposite conclusion, finding that public organizations are frequently terminated. These findings largely relate to contexts where changes to the ruling party occur regularly. In contrast, this study examines the survival of government agencies in Japan, where the postwar political system has been characterized by one‐party dominance and short‐lived political leadership. The findings suggest that Japanese agencies remain largely “immortal,” and that when they do undergo transitions this tends to be linked to prime ministers with longer tenures who are able to implement minor, cosmetic changes; hence agencies typically persist even after such events. This study thus sheds new light on how political–administrative relations shape patterns of agency transition and highlights the importance of leadership tenure in sustaining commitments to organizational change.

title: Emulate the Leader? Explaining Crisis Policy Change in the Canadian Federal System
abstract: In times of crises, do governments coordinate or do they make their own choices independent of what others do? Convergence of COVID‐19 policy at the beginning of the pandemic has been widely studied in federal countries. Yet, there is limited literature looking at the mechanisms that made policy between jurisdictions so similar. Utilizing Canada's decentralized federal system, this paper posits that convergence can be explained by a process of policy diffusion through emulation and a series of leader‐follower relationships. Drawing on the policy diffusion literature, this paper proposes three hypotheses for why some jurisdictions take on leadership roles in crisis policy while others follow. Synthesized as proximity, capacity, and urgency, these hypotheses are tested using a series of pairwise vector autoregressions identifying significant leader‐follower relationships between Canadian provinces. The findings suggest that policy primarily flowed from only a small number of large provinces (Quebec and Ontario), lending partial evidence, but also exceptions to the hypotheses proposed.

abstract: We introduce retrieval-augmented surveys, a novel survey approach that links respondents’ open-ended priorities to concrete policy proposals in institutional databases, enabling personalized measures of how citizens’ concerns map onto formal agendas. Our pipeline elicits and clarifies each respondent’s top issue concern, summarizes items in a policy database and retrieves semantically relevant candidates (“nearest neighbors”) for inclusion in a respondent-tailored survey. We illustrate the approach with an application to political representation in Congress, evaluating performance across four metrics. First, large majorities of respondents judge the retrieved policy items as mostly or fully addressing their concerns. Second, a hand-coding audit corroborates the alignment of retrieved items with respondent issue stances. Third, support for retrieved items is stable over a short-term panel, with 82% of respondents at the top of the support scale remaining there three weeks later. Fourth, in a tailored conjoint, alignment on the nearest neighbor item has a larger estimated effect on candidate choice than benchmark policies. The framework is modular and portable to other settings, such as rulemaking, municipal agendas, and public budgets, enabling scholars to identify where representation succeeds or fails in the institutional pipeline.

title: Euclidean Ideal Point Estimation from Roll-Call Data via Distance-Based Bipartite Network Models
authors: Seungju Lee, In Kyun Kim, Jong Hee Park, Ick Hoon Jin
abstract: Conventional ideal point models rely on Gaussian or quadratic utility functions that violate the triangle inequality, producing non-metric distances that complicate geometric interpretation and undermine clustering and dispersion-based analyses. We introduce a distance-based alternative that adapts the latent space item response model (LSIRM) to roll-call data, treating legislators and bills as nodes in a bipartite network jointly embedded in a Euclidean metric space. Through controlled simulations, Euclidean LSIRM consistently recovers latent coalition structure with superior cluster separation relative to existing methods. Applied to the 118th U.S. House, the model provides competitive predictive performance while yielding bill embeddings that clarify cross-cutting issue alignments. The results show that restoring metric structure to ideal point estimation provides a clearer and more coherent inference about party cohesion, factional divisions and multidimensional legislative behavior.

title: How Accurate Are Survey Measurements of Objective Phenomena?
authors: Lisanne Wichgers, Linchiat Chang, David Chapman, Elizabeth Elder, Jon Krosnick, Matt Berent, Amanda Scott, Elaine Albertson, Elizabeth Quinlan
abstract: How accurate are survey measurements of phenomena that can be objectively verified? This article reports a review of various types of evidence assessing accuracy (vs. benchmarks not derived from self-reports) across a wide spectrum of content areas, including demographics, healthcare, labor force statistics, substance use and more. The vast majority of measurements were accurate, according to three assessment methods. Individual respondents’ self-reports closely matched objective records of the same phenomena for the same individual. Small aggregate differences were observed between survey sample means and aggregate means derived from objective records. Self-reports correlated strongly with measures of the same attributes of those individuals from secondary data not based on self-reports. Taken together, the evidence suggests that survey measurements of objective phenomena are highly accurate.

title: An Image Is Worth K Topics: A Visual Structural Topic Model with Pretrained Image Embeddings
authors: Matías Piqueras, Alexandra Segerberg, Matteo Magnani, Måns Magnusson, Nataša Sladoje
abstract: Political scientists are increasingly interested in analyzing visual content at scale. However, the existing computational toolbox is still in need of methods and models attuned to the specific challenges and goals of social and political inquiry. In this article, we introduce a visual structural topic model (vSTM) that combines continuous image embeddings with a structural topic model. This has important advantages compared to existing approaches. First, continuous embeddings allow the model to capture the semantic complexity of images, which is relevant to the study of politics. A consequence of using continuous embeddings is that we can directly use off-the-shelf pretrained deep learning models, offering state-of-the-art performance in image analysis tasks while saving time, cost and resources. Second, the structural topic model provides the ability to analyze how topics and covariates are related, while maintaining a nuanced representation of images as a mixture of multiple topics. In our experiments, we show that the vSTM is able to identify topics that are interpretable, coherent and relevant to the study of online political communication.

title: The Effect of Clients’ Financial Resources, Mental Health, and Motivation on Frontline Workers’ Burden Reduction and Prioritizations
authors: Niels Bjørn Grund Petersen, Jonas Krogh Madsen
abstract: The street-level bureaucracy literature shows that frontline workers’ decisions about clients are shaped by perceptions of deservingness based on clients’ demographic characteristics and behavioral conduct. Yet, we know little about whether frontline workers also act on clients’ financial resources and mental health, despite the administrative burden literature identifying these two factors as central to how citizens experience compliance demands. We contribute to both literatures by developing and testing preregistered hypotheses that examine how information about clients’ financial resources and mental health shapes frontline workers’ burden reduction and client prioritization. To do this, we run a large-scale vignette experiment with 775 caseworkers across 39 Danish unemployment agencies, manipulating client age, financial situation, mental health, and motivation but holding gender constant (all clients were male). We find strong evidence that caseworkers reduce burdens and prioritize clients with mental health issues and–consistent with prior work–clients displaying high motivation, alongside some evidence for clients struggling with financial hardship. Importantly, mental health appears more consequential than motivation and financial resources. Contrary to our preregistered expectation, clients with mental health issues received the most support when they also displayed low as opposed to high motivation. Rather than indicating that frontline workers reward low motivation, this pattern most likely reflects that caseworkers interpret low motivation as a symptom of the underlying condition, and thus as a signal of greater need. Our findings show how frontline discretion can operate as a redistributive mechanism that channels support toward clients signaling the greatest need.

title: Toward an “Identity Turn” in Public Service Motivation Theory: A Problematizing Review and Research Agenda
abstract: Since its inception, Public Service Motivation (PSM) has been recognized as a key driver of behavior in public institutions. Despite its prominence, skepticism has emerged. In response, research has primarily focused on empirical analysis and measurement refinement rather than on conceptual development. This conceptual path dependency has become problematic as mixed empirical results increasingly challenge core theoretical propositions of PSM theory. We argue that one potential cause lies in a dominant assumption shaping the field: its positioning within motivation theory. To address this, we conducted a problematizing review across concepts and disciplines, comparing how PSM is understood in Public Administration with related concepts–such as motivation, altruism, and identity–in Management, Psychology, Sociology, and Economics. Based on this analysis, we propose a novel theoretical framework that reconceptualizes PSM as a social identity. In doing so, we outline a research agenda that (i) revises PSM’s core conceptual features and develops a new measurement approach informed by identity theory; (ii) introduces new ways of understanding PSM's functioning through identity work theory; and (iii) situates PSM theory within the broader debate on the “identity turn” in motivation research, highlighting its potential contribution to this multidisciplinary discourse.

title: Agrarian revolt or populist disruption? The breakthrough of the farmer-citizen-movement (BBB) in the Netherlands
authors: Simon Otjes, Thereza Langeler, Léonie de Jonge
abstract: Founded in 2019, the Dutch Farmer-Citizen-Movement ( BoerBurgerBeweging , BBB) has emerged as a significant force in Dutch politics. In a highly urbanized country, the rise of an explicitly rurally oriented political party is striking. We analyze the origins of the BBB, seeking to explain its electoral breakthrough. Using the frameworks of agrarianism and agrarian populism, we assess whether the BBB represents a revival of either tradition. Using qualitative and quantitative methods, we examine the party’s rhetoric and voter base in its founding years. Our findings indicate that the BBB adapted agrarian populist ideological tenets to fit the 21 st century context in which it operated. It initially mobilized around opposition to environmental policy and regional resentment, while valorizing rural life and expressing distrust of political elites. The BBB illustrates how populism can be reshaped through agrarian concerns, deepening the cleavage between the urban center and the rural periphery.

title: Campaigning on emotion: Party strategy and emotional appeals in the 2024 UK general election
authors: Iván Sánchez-Marañón, Jordi Rodríguez-Virgili, Miguel Gómez-Irimia
abstract: Purpose: This article examines how political parties used emotional appeals in campaign advertising during the 2024 United Kingdom general election. Methods: Through content analysis of ads published by the Conservative Party, Labour, the Liberal Democrats, and Reform UK across their main social media platforms, we identify party-level patterns in emotional strategy and the conditions shaping their use. Findings: The Conservative Party relied heavily on fear, consistent with its trailing incumbent status. Labour led on anger, directing appeals almost exclusively at the Conservative governing record, while also deploying enthusiasm around the promise of change. Reform UK and the Liberal Democrats made the most frequent use of enthusiasm. Across all parties, enthusiasm targeted the ingroup, while anger and fear targeted the outgroup. Conclusions: These findings align with theoretical expectations derived from incumbency status and poll position across a full field of competing parties in a single campaign, providing evidence that electoral periods fuel affective polarisation.

title: Keep the peace? The early politics of Covid-19 and the limits of partisan influence on public opinion
authors: Franziska Graf, Alexa Lenz, Christian Adam
abstract: Crises often call for swift and far-reaching government action that depends on broad public acceptance to be effective. While political disagreement is commonly seen as undermining support, its actual impact on public attitudes remains contested. This study examines public opinion during the COVID-19 pandemic in Germany – a context that shifted from early cross-party unity to later politicization. Combining original media data on partisan messaging and panel survey data from 2020, we assess how the emergence of partisan criticism shaped public acceptance of pandemic response policies. Although increasing partisan politicization was associated with declining public acceptance of pandemic measures, we find no evidence that this relationship was driven by partisan cue-taking. Instead, citizens adjusted their party preferences rather than their policy views in response to disagreement with their preferred party. These findings highlight the limits of partisan persuasion, and the growing importance of citizens’ own evaluations as elite consensus erodes.

title: The Pied Piper of 4chan : Fairy-tale narratives of racist and misogynistic radicalisation in UK elite political discourse
abstract: UK political elites increasingly represent racist and misogynistic violence as a problem of ‘radicalisation’ in which, like the Pied Piper luring the children of Hamelin, predatory online ‘radicalisers’ lure and brainwash susceptible youth. This article examines how this narrative achieves dominance despite the availability of empirically grounded alternatives, asking what role narrative form plays in its success. Through a narrative analysis of UK counterterrorism policies and parliamentary statements, it reconstructs the narrative’s setting, characterisation and emplotment, demonstrating significant resemblances with several popular fairy tales. The article argues that this intertextual resonance with culturally embedded story forms lends the ‘radicalisation’ narrative a familiarity and coherence that alternative narratives – which foreground the everyday settings, adult perpetrators and structural persistence of these harms – lack. The article concludes by suggesting that contesting the ‘radicalisation’ narrative’s dominance requires telling counter-stories of comparable verisimilitude rather than simply assembling better evidence.

title: Regimes of violence/nonviolence: regulating the meaning-making of violence and nonviolence
abstract: Despite the growth in violence and nonviolence literature, few scholars explore how the meanings of these terms are governed, disregarding their discursive character. Expanding on the revived ‘regime of violence’ theory, this article proposes the concept of regime of violence/nonviolence as an inclusive and comprehensive conceptualisation that entangles violence, nonviolence, and their relations. States reify hegemonic regimes of violence that regulate and reinforce commonsensical state-legitimising understandings of violence. By co-opting nonviolence scholars and institutions, they attempt to do the same with a strategic, statist and reformist notion of nonviolence based on a politics of respectability. Contesting these dominant notions, resistance groups and critical scholars advance alternative understandings of violence and nonviolence that can reify counter-hegemonic regimes of violence/nonviolence. The concept of a regime of violence/nonviolence brings together violence and nonviolence scholarship and can enable more situated, empirical studies of how the meanings and practices of violence and nonviolence are governed.

title: Paid, but not a partner: Monetization without standing in Facebook’s Performance Bonus Program
abstract: Platform revenue-sharing programs both pay and govern creators. Drawing on interviews with 18 participants in Facebook’s Performance Bonus Program (PBP) and the author’s own participation, this study examines how monetization reshaped creators’ platform governance expectations. PBP’s onboarding, which addressed recipients as “valued creators” and promised earnings of “up to $30,000 a month,” combined with early recurring payouts to cultivate expectations of continuity and institutional responsiveness, particularly among participants new to monetization. When enforcement errors, payout volatility, and support failures followed, participants discovered that payment had not conferred meaningful access to explanation, human review, or recourse. This article theorizes that condition as monetization without standing : a governance arrangement in which creators are compensated and governed as laborers while denied the procedural recognition typically associated with paid work. This arrangement constitutes a breach of the psychological contract generated by monetization, producing durable behavioral constraint, disparate impacts on marginalized creators, and creator attrition.

title: Fuck You, Pay Me: Payment apps, review platforms, and ambivalent resistance in the influencer industry
abstract: This article critically examines emerging intermediaries in the influencer industry that aggregate anonymous reviews of brands and allow influencers to report how much they were paid. Turning to four intermediaries (Fuck You Pay Me, Willa, Hashtag Pay Me, and Clara for Creators), I argue that although these emerging intermediaries represent an important step toward creating more equity, these efforts are a double-edged sword and represent a form of ambivalent resistance to broader structures governing the influencer industry. While these intermediaries are used to resist the precarity of platformized and branded cultural production, these transactions have the potential to be co-opted—used for surveillance and data tracking by brands, platforms, and corporations—potentially blunting emerging forms of collective action and solidarity. Ultimately, these intermediaries provide an opportunity to theorize forms of resistance to precarity as neither “top-down” nor “bottom-up,” but rather a means of negotiating and navigating power from limited and precarious positions.

title: Ambivalence and antagonism: The intertwinement of gossiping and public shaming on social media
abstract: The vernacular practices of public shaming and gossiping on social media function both as entertainment and as disciplinary mechanisms. This article investigates two Finnish subreddits on Reddit, where gossiping and public shaming practices are closely intertwined. On these subreddits, screenshots of Finnish social media content creators’ posts are intensely circulated, scrutinised and dissected. This article examines how the gossiping practices are tied to the vernacular practices of public shaming on social media and what these practices are affixed to within the discourses created on these subreddits. The study found that the entertainment and judgement derived from these practices are tethered to themes of unpredictability, ambivalence and community building. These create moral discourses about non-normative ways of self-presentation and public conduct, both in corporal and online realms. Moreover, this study exemplifies that when gossiping and public shaming on social media intertwine, the line between disciplining and bullying becomes easier to cross.

abstract: We present a comparative case study of software development teams in 14 firms, based on 50 semi-structured interviews with 39 people, plus non-participant observation. Our theory proposes that an inherent contradiction of labour management—conflicting pressures to empower workers (to enhance capabilities) and to control workers (to ensure labour discipline)—becomes refracted in distinct ways through the service triangle between customers, managers, and workers. We ask how do software managers deal with competing pressures to simultaneously (1) generate high-quality, creative output, (2) ensure efficiency and workforce discipline, and (3) mediate between clients and workers? Most managers in our study primarily focused on empowering their software developers while the latter experienced client attempts to establish detailed control of their work. In these cases, the managers attempted to control the clients by buffering developers from client demands or pushing back against them.

title: When climate change enters the market: California wildfires and the homeowners insurance crisis
abstract: Homeowners insurance is central to the functioning of mortgage and housing markets, but climate change threatens the conditions on which this role has been built. This study examines this tension in California, asking: how does climate change reshape underwriting practices in the homeowners insurance market, and which communities are most affected by these changes? Leveraging ZIP Code-level data, I show that the relationship between wildfire risk and insurance outcomes changed discontinuously after the disastrous 2017–2018 wildfire season, with high-risk areas experiencing a sharp spike in coverage loss followed by a subsequent increase in reliance on insurance of last resort. Moreover, the findings point to the unequal distributional consequences of this new form of climate vulnerability: coverage loss and reliance on insurance of last resort are systematically higher in lower-income areas, suggesting that financial vulnerability overlaps with a higher risk of inadequate coverage. Taken together, the findings show that the short-term structure of insurance contracts can turn prolonged increases in climate risk—periods of “risk accumulation”—into discontinuous economic shocks, adding a further layer of unequally distributed disruption beyond direct disaster damage.

title: When investment becomes religion: anxiety, quasi-religious practices, and household financialization
abstract: In recent years, household investors have been increasingly drawn to highly volatile financial assets, particularly among younger demographics. This trend generates what I call dual anxiety: the tension between precarity-induced anxiety that pulls individuals into financial markets as a necessary strategy for securing their future and volatility-induced anxiety that threatens to push them out through repeated losses. How do household investors navigate this dual anxiety? Drawing on forty-one interviews with South Korean Tesla retail shareholders and 20 months of digital ethnography in online investment communities, I find that dual anxiety fosters quasi-religious practices among some investors. These practices include: (1) performing daily rituals of faith, (2) searching for charismatic authority, and (3) deferring the promised salvation. These practices accompany household investors’ continued purchasing of more shares despite losses. This research contributes to the financialization literature by illuminating the underexplored religious elements within modern investment life through which household financialization sustains and reproduces itself.

title: An Informational Letter From the Federal Government Increases Naturalization Submissions
authors: Oded Gurantz, Amanda Girard, Elisa Cascardi, Sofia Avila, Tomás R. Jiménez
abstract: Citizenship offers enhanced opportunities for immigrants, but the complex naturalization process can be a barrier. We evaluate a preregistered, large‐scale randomized trial that tested the impact of a low‐cost letter that combined informational content with active encouragement from the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to potentially eligible Lawful Permanent Residents (LPRs) to apply for naturalization. Within a nationwide population of 1,861,178 individuals in LPR status for 6 to 9 years, we find that the letter increased naturalization applications by 1 percentage point (12%). This increase was positive across all groups tested, though the effects were larger for families in higher income zip codes and those who did not submit the fee waiver application, suggesting that financial and time constraints, along with administrative burdens, play a role in naturalization submission rates.

title: Is the Territorial Integrity Norm in Its Death Throes?
abstract: The territorial integrity norm, designed to safeguard states against forcible redrawing of their borders and for decades regarded as foundational to the post-1945 global order, has been repeatedly challenged since 2008. These developments have led commentators to suggest that the norm is undergoing significant weakening or even outright extinction. The assumption informing these assertions is that norm strength internationally is determined by (1) the frequency of violations, (2) the relative power of violators, (3) the effectiveness of enforcement measures by third parties in countering violations, or (4) some combination of the three. In contrast, I argue that the territorial integrity norm has not markedly eroded. Norms are socially held ideas about proper behavior rather than patterns of actual behavior. A norm can be undone only by a collective abandonment of its underlying idea, not by individual infringements or ineffective enforcement. Its strength is the extent to which social commitment to it persists. The necessary empirical indicator of that commitment is concordance: public affirmation of norms, especially in cases of norm breaking. Although supplementing concordance with material measures to counter norm-breaking constitutes additional evidence of that commitment, norm strength is not contingent on the success of these efforts, which may prove elusive even when they entail substantial material coercion. Norm strength is undermined not by international society’s inability to restore the status quo ante when violations occur, but by its failure to call them violations and to continually repudiate them in the first place. In the case of territorial integrity, concordance has been most compellingly expressed by third-party refusals to recognize the forcible acquisition of territory as a valid transfer of sovereignty. In line with the pre-2008 practice, the recent attempts at, or formal backing of, such territorial acquisitions have, overall, continued to elicit sweeping refusals to extend recognition.

Embodying Hope: Choreographies of Presence and Reiterative Endurance in Latin American Feminist Protest
authors: Camila Páez-Bernal, Maša Mrovlje, Jennet Kirkpatrick
abstract: How is hope sustained under conditions of violence, loss, and political disappointment? Recent feminist and critical theorists have reimagined hope as entangled with grief and failure, yet this work remains largely focused on texts and representation. In this article, we develop a feminist theory of embodied hope grounded in Latin American feminist protest. Drawing on interviews and ethnographic and visual documentation from Colombia and Mexico (2022–23), we show how activists enact hope through what we call choreographies of presence: collective acts of public visibility, such as mourning, dance, mutual aid, and bodily exposure. We argue that these practices reframe feminist hope as a collective, democratic capacity for endurance grounded in return, relationality, and a refusal of closure. Rather than deferring hope to a future horizon, these movements sustain political life by returning to sites of loss and enduring together.

Comparative Politics and the New Area Studies
authors: Jordan Gans-Morse, Daniel W. Gingerich, Thomas B. Pepinsky
abstract: In the 1990s, a sharp divide emerged between area studies advocates and methodologically oriented political scientists. We revisit that debate, arguing that tensions between political science and area studies are neither intrinsic nor static but instead evolve in tandem with theoretical and methodological trends, as well as with broader political and technological developments. Drawing on an original survey of American Political Science Association members and an analysis of roughly 4,500 comparative politics articles in leading journals, we identify four shifts in the discipline: from a theoretical to an empirical orientation, from cross-national datasets to country- and region-specific studies, from macro- to micro-level analyses, and from descriptive to causal inference. We also document evolving patterns in language training, fieldwork, methods use, and data collection. Our findings suggest that political science and area studies are experiencing a reconciliation, but that the state of area studies is fragile and the subdiscipline of comparative politics must support it.

title: The Distributional Impacts of Time-Varying Electricity Pricing: A Novel Approach to Estimating Household Income,
authors: Mar Reguant, Natalia Fabra, Jingyuan Wang
abstract: As interest in the distributional effects of climate policies gains prominence, designing electricity tariffs that are both efficient and equitable becomes critical. Efficiency often favors the shift from time-invariant to time-of-use (ToU) or real-time prices (RTP), but this transition may have distributional implications. We develop a framework to assess the implications and the channels through which distributional impacts manifest. Central to our approach is a novel method that infers individual household income by combining zip-code-level income data with household-level electricity consumption. We demonstrate the value of this method in the Spanish context. First, we show that using more granular estimates of income has an impact on the distributional assessment of electricity tariffs. Second, we find that the potential distributional impact of RTP is very modest compared to the impact of ToU. The most salient effect of RTP is to increase bill volatility, particularly so for the low-income group.

title: The Scope of Statistical Discrimination: An Experimental Study on Gender Barriers in Tech,
authors: Jan Feld, Edwin Ip, Andreas Leibbrandt, Joseph Vecci
abstract: Women are significantly underrepresented in the technology sector. We design an experimental study using field data to identify the role of statistical discrimination in job applicant assessments. First, we measure the programming skills of job applicants for a programming job. Then, we recruit a large sample of employers consisting of human resource and tech professionals and incentivize them to predict the performance of these applicants based on their standardized resumes. We find no significant gender differences in programming skills. However, consistent with statistical discrimination we find employers perceive female applicants to be significantly less skilled. We also provide experimental evidence that the perceived gender skill gap can be readily eliminated. Employers who were randomized to have access to additional information such as aptitude or personality do not believe that there are gender differences in programming skills. Together, these findings suggest that tech employers believe women are less skilled programmers. Nonetheless, in the context of hiring, the scope for statistical discrimination may be limited in practice as employers often have access to more information when assessing applicants.

title: Pork, Infrastructure and Growth: Evidence from the Italian Railway Expansion,
authors: Roberto Bonfatti, Giovanni Facchini, Alexander Tarasov, Gian Luca Tedeschi, Cecilia Testa
abstract: We study the political economy of transport infrastructure placement and its long-term impact, exploiting quasi-random variation in political factors. Using unique data from XIX-century Italy and deploying a regression discontinuity design, we focus on close races to show that towns in marginal districts supporting winning candidates were more likely to be reached by a railway. Using alignment with the government as a natural instrument for infrastructure placement, we then show that over the following century, services - rather than manufacturing - grew faster in connected municipalities. Our results also indicate that political allegiances likely helped towns with lower growth prospects.

title: The Political Economy of Propaganda: Evidence from US Newspapers,
abstract: This study examines whether racial outrage in the media can result from the incentives of elites who seek to divide society for political gain, focusing on the late 19th century Southern United States. At this time, the Democratic Party had strong political incentives to incite racial outrage, and local Democratic elites exercised considerable influence over newspapers, the only mass media at the time. Using high-frequency historical newspaper data and difference-in-differences and triple-difference estimation strategies, we find evidence consistent with Democratic elites orchestrating a racist propaganda campaign to sway white voters. Supporting analyses are consistent with Democrats benefiting from anti-Black propaganda in the subsequent elections.

title: Perceived Political Bias of the Federal Reserve,
authors: Pei Kuang, Michael Weber, Shihan Xie
abstract: We conduct a survey experiment with a politically representative sample of more than 5,000 U.S. consumers to study how perceptions of the Federal Reserve’s (Fed) political stance shape macroeconomic expectations, trust, and information processing. Overall, 63.5% of respondents view the Fed as politically neutral, 9.4% as aligned with their own party (in-group), and 27.2% as opposed (out-group). The non-neutral minority differs sharply: out-group respondents report substantially higher inflation expectations and lower trust than neutral or in-group respondents, even after controlling for partisanship and demographics. They also pay more to avoid opposing media and are less likely to receive Fed communication—yet update their expectations by more once exposed to it, placing less weight on their priors when the same article carries a Fed label. In a hypothetical Trump presidency, the neutral share falls to 37.2%, with respondents in both parties shifting toward viewing the Fed as Republican-leaning, consistent with expected political capture. Perceived neutrality is thus central to the Fed’s credibility and the reach of its communication, and it can shift with changes in political leadership.

title: Spatial Restructuring, Labour Reallocation, and Household Income: Evidence From Poverty Alleviation Resettlement in China
authors: Wei Ouyang, Xin Qi, Mengmin Sun, Ziyang Chen, Yixiao Zhu, Yang Zhou
abstract: China's poverty alleviation resettlement (PAR) programme provides an opportunity to examine how state‐led population redistribution reshapes rural household livelihoods. Drawing on 186,705 household‐year observations from Fuping County eastern China, between 2014 and 2022, we estimate a two‐way fixed‐effects difference‐in‐differences model and conduct robustness checks that account for staggered treatment timing. PAR improves access to several public services but increases the distance between homes and cultivated land. It is associated with an approximately 1.1% increase in household per‐capita net income. Mechanism‐consistent estimates indicate that PAR increases non‐agricultural employment, with the employment response concentrated within the resettlement township rather than at more distant locations. PAR also increases the annual duration of non‐agricultural employment. Income gains are larger among female‐headed households and households with skilled workers, but smaller among households with higher shares of older members. Income outcomes also vary by resettlement destination and type of post‐relocation support. By distinguishing sectoral labour reallocation from geographical labour mobility, the study shows how state‐led population redistribution can facilitate economic mobility through highly localised labour‐market integration without necessarily increasing long‐distance migration. It contributes to population geography by demonstrating that the developmental consequences of relocation depend on how access to employment, services and productive land is reorganised, as well as on households’ differing capacities to take advantage of these opportunities. Our findings demonstrate that PAR achieves spatial restructuring, labor reallocation, livelihood strategy reshaping, and livelihood sustainability, and represents an important initiative for eliminating long‐term (chronic) poverty resulting from geo‐environmental constraints.

The Epistemic Double Bind of Parity Representation in France’s National Assembly
abstract: As legislatures approach gender parity in different parts of the world, questions remain about whether institutional cultures support equal epistemic authority for women. In the French National Assembly, modern republicanism promotes depersonalized representation: deputies are expected to embody the universal citizen, with gender embedded but not defining. Drawing on 24 interviews with deputies elected before and after the 2017 elections, this article develops a feminist institutionalist framework to show how women navigate tensions between republican expectations that demand conformity to masculinized neutrality and pluralist norms that confine authority to “women’s issues.” We introduce the concept of epistemic double bind to theorize this dilemma and present a typology of role expectations and strategic responses that captures how deputies negotiate it. Our findings show that even in more gender-balanced legislatures, women face enduring constraints on epistemic authority. France serves as a critical case for understanding the practical demands of depersonalized representation and how actors reconfigure its contradictions in institutions shaped by parity laws.

title: Judicial Storytelling and the Political Construction of Abortion in State Courts
abstract: In the wake of the United States Supreme Court decision, Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization (2022), state courts have emerged as central sites for contesting and redefining abortion. Existing scholarship on abortion storytelling has focused largely on individuals, advocates, and legislators, emphasizing how personal narratives shape public opinion and policymaking. This essay shifts analytic attention to a less visible but highly consequential set of narrators: courts. It argues that judicial opinions do more than resolve legal disputes; they are institutional stories that construct abortion’s meaning.

Regulatory Rationales in the Face of Emerging Technologies: A Systematic Review
abstract: Technology is evolving, and so is the discussion of regulation theory among academics. Taking a unique approach to legal research, this paper utilizes the systematic literature review methodology to uncover quantitative evidence on the current consensus among academics on regulation theory, in particular, regulatory rationales. This paper seeks to determine whether the narrative assumptions that social solidarity‐based regulatory rationales have become more prevalent as technology has evolved are correct. Based on the data gathered, this article asserts that the discussion of regulatory rationales is facing a tonal shift as a result of artificial intelligence. Academics are shifting away from a traditional economic view of regulation toward discussion of regulatory rationales based on protecting the common good. This should be welcome. Social solidarity should serve as a foundational principle of good technology regulation. Through applying the principles of social solidarity, regulators can better balance the risks and benefits of modern technology.

title: How Europeans view and evaluate democracy at the European level
authors: Hanspeter Kriesi, Ben Crum, Chendi Wang
abstract: This exploratory study asks how Europeans view EU democracy and how satisfied they are with how EU democracy works. Roughly one-fifth of them do not appear to have any idea about democracy at the EU level. We create a typology of European democrats distinguishing between allegiant, delegative, assertive, and disaffected democrats, show the distribution over the types, and analyze the factors associated with its two dimensions and the types. Citizens’ opinions on EU democracy deviate most notably from their views on national democracy in that much fewer of them want to expand it. As expected, pro-Europeans demand more democracy and are more satisfied with EU democracy than Euroskeptics. Feeling represented at the EU level and trusting EU institutions most strongly enhances demand for and satisfaction with EU democracy. In general, Europeans have clearer ideas about how democracy works in the EU than about how they want it to work.

title: Book Review: The Backstage of Democracy: India’s Election Campaigns and the People Who Manage Them by Sharma, A. SharmaA. (2025). The Backstage of Democracy: India’s Election Campaigns and the People Who Manage Them. Cambridge University Press. 358 pp, $130 (Hardback). ISBN: 9781009423984.
The Articulation Loop: State Signaling, Platform Infrastructures, and User Weaponization in China's Qinglang Era
abstract: This article examines how Qinglang (Clear and Bright), China's campaign‐based discourse of internet content governance, sustains regulatory force as its meaning shifts across state, platform, and user domains. It develops the articulation loop as a mechanism for explaining how a state‐authored yet semantically open signifier acquires practical force through its connections to institutional authority, platform governance infrastructures, organized user practices, and selective regulatory recalibration. Drawing on articulation theory and adaptive governance, the article traces Qinglang across three domains. At the state level, Qinglang operates as a floating signifier through which changing governance problems can be periodically named, sequenced, and recentralized in special campaigns. At the platform level, platforms bind Qinglang to rules, reporting channels, visibility controls, and rectification procedures, while enforcement remains commercially calibrated. At the user level, organized fans weaponize Qinglang‐linked compliance categories to reframe peer conflicts, seek visibility penalties, and conduct reverse audits of platform accountability. The article conceptualizes Qinglang‐era content governance as a form of state‐led multistakeholderism, in which participation by platforms and users is organized within a state‐defined normative order that makes participation selectively actionable while preserving final authority at the state level.

title: Distributed range adaptation in human parietal encoding of numbers
authors: Arthur Prat-Carrabin, Gilles de Hollander, Saurabh Bedi, Samuel J. Gershman, Christian C. Ruff
abstract: The brain’s representations are encoded in the collective activity of neural populations whose non-monotonic tuning properties define the population code. Adaptive behavior calls for flexible retuning of this code as stimulus statistics change across contexts. Yet how such adaptation occurs is unknown. Using fMRI during a numerosity-estimation task with variable number ranges, we show that number representations in human parietal cortex dynamically recalibrate to context, enabling context-sensitive behavioral accuracy. The tuning properties of neural populations collectively shift and rescale with the range. This distributed range adaptation achieves efficient coding in real time: neural precision scales with the range and predicts corresponding changes in behavioral precision. Individuals with stronger neural adaptation show larger behavioral adjustments. These findings extend static sensory efficient coding to adaptive representations of abstract magnitudes. Such flexible population tuning may constitute a canonical mechanism of encoding networks that enables the brain to sustain precise, adaptive behavior.

title: Partisan responsiveness in real time: causal evidence from Trump’s military attack on Iran
authors: Stuart J. Turnbull-Dugarte, Peter Luca Versteegen, Daniel Devine, Owen Winter
abstract: Elite cues signal citizens how to interpret political events through a partisan lens. Do these effects occur in real time? We exploit President Trump’s unexpected announcement of US military strikes against Iran during a nationally representative survey to estimate the causal effect of elite cues on public opinion. Leveraging minute-level variation in exposure, we find that partisan divergence emerges almost immediately: support for military intervention increases among Republicans but declines among Democrats. These large effects remain robust across 28,672 model specifications and 57,344 partisan-specific treatment effects. Our quasi-experimental evidence demonstrates that elite cues can polarize public opinion within minutes, even before media framing and partisan commentary have diffused, highlighting the speed of partisan opinion formation and its implications for democratic accountability.

title: Government ideology and gender equality in public sector career progression
authors: Lasse Aaskoven, Benjamin C.K. Egerod, Frederik K. Kjøller
abstract: Why are women underrepresented in civil service management across rich democracies? We argue that government ideology matters for this question, and that women bureaucrats’ careers stagnate under right-wing governments, since they do not suppress gender-inequality-reinforcing promotion patterns. We examine this using administrative occupation data on all Danish central government employees, observed quarterly from 1998 to 2019. The evidence is consistent with our argument: Under left-wing governments, men and women in the civil service progress similarly, while women progress more slowly than men under right-wing governments. The gender gap in career progression widens at the higher echelons of the bureaucracy, where political attention is greater, and this gap is not reduced by the presence of women ministers.

title: Is alliance credibility interdependent?
abstract: How might changes in the credibility of one alliance relate to the credibility of other alliance commitments? Debate between competing views on this question spans decades in part because systematic tests are difficult. We contribute systematic evidence with a new measure of credibility in U.S. alliances and novel technique to estimate interdependence. Our measure draws on expert ratings of allied beliefs over U.S. credibility and our analysis employs Gaussian process regression to analyze credibility. We find strong correlations in allied credibility perceptions within regions and little correlation across regions. Supplementary analyses suggest that these correlations reflect common unobservables and a small impact of shared perception of past U.S. behavior.

title: Educational polarization: evidence from the White House staff
authors: Kenneth Lowande, Saloni Singh, Abigail Paegert, Alan Andrade
abstract: American political polarization has mapped onto educational pedigree, with credentialed elites increasingly supporting Democrats. We examine the implications of this trend in the most powerful office in American politics: the White House. From 1995 to 2024, we show Democratic presidents employed staffs with higher educational attainment, and that Republicans were more likely to attend public institutions, those without R1 status, and those ranked below the top 50%. We then show that universities whose alumni disproportionately went on to work for Democratic presidents were more likely to face investigations, enforcement actions, and funding cuts after President Trump took office in 2025. Our findings suggest educational pedigree among staff who operate key political institutions warrant further investigation.

title: Panel data on mobility, socio-economic, and political impacts of riverbank erosion and flooding in Bangladesh
authors: Jan Freihardt, Lukas Rudolph, Vally Koubi
abstract: We present the Bangladesh Environmental Mobility Panel (BEMP), a household panel along Bangladesh’s Jamuna River that traces the impacts of riverbank erosion and flooding on (im)mobility, including short- and long-distance movements, socio-economic outcomes, and political attitudes. The dataset follows 1,691 households with a total of 2,170 panel respondents from 2021–2024 through four annual in-person survey waves and ten phone survey waves at two- to six-month intervals, yielding 24,279 completed surveys with low attrition. Respondent selection via a spatially randomized draw supports inference to households in sampling villages at risk of erosion along the 250 km eastern bank of the Jamuna River. Migrants were tracked, and the plausibly exogenous timing of erosion, conditional on sampling zone and location, provides leverage for research designs linking environmental shocks to mobility. Surveys include measures of socio-demographics, livelihoods, economic outcomes and well-being, conflict and cooperation, and political attitudes, supporting questions in development economics and politics in a rural Global South setting. The design enables gender- and age-sensitive analyses by providing data on household heads (n = 1,691), additional senior female (n = 269) and youth (n = 210) respondents, and left-behind members of migrating-head households (n = 273), complemented by village profiles, focus group discussions, and qualitative interviews with women.

title: A cross-sectional psychometric and demographic dataset of adolescents at high-risk for suicide
authors: José Manuel Ramírez-Sánchez, Mario Manso-Vázquez, Beatriz Gómez-Gómez, María Sánchez-Luaces, Alexandre Filgueiras-Rodríguez, Karla Alexis Caballero-Bello, Sabela Armesto-Iglesias, Antía Brañas-Gonzalez, Icía María Nistal-Franco, María Ozaita-Corral, Sara Ferreiro-González, Tania Rivera-Baltanas, María Tajes-Alonso, Carlos Spuch, Manuel José Fernández-Iglesias, Laura Docío-Fernández, Carmen García-Mateo, Alejandro A. García-Caballero
abstract: This data descriptor presents a dataset containing demographic and psychometric information from 207 adolescents aged 12 to 17. The data were collected as part of a three-group, cross-sectional study design. The sample includes a High-Risk Group (HR-G) (N=43) of adolescents recently admitted for an acute suicidal crisis; a Psychiatric Control Group (PC-G) (N=55) receiving care for non-suicidal conditions; and a General Control Group (GC-G) (N=109) with no known psychiatric history. Data collection includes sociodemographic variables (age, sex, school grade) and item-level responses alongside aggregated scores from seven validated self-report instruments. The assessment includes suicidal ideation, general mental health difficulties, depressive symptoms, bullying, cyberbullying, and problematic internet use. This dataset provides a valuable resource for researchers in psychiatry, psychology, statistics and machine learning to investigate the psychological factors associated with adolescent suicidality and develop predictive models for risk assessment.

title: Political institutions and public opinion on abortion decisions post-Dobbs
authors: Jeong Hyun Kim, Nichole Bauer, Anna Gunderson
abstract: At a time when state institutions are increasingly setting abortion policy through different channels, understanding which decision-making processes the public views as legitimate has crucial consequences for democratic governance and public trust in democratic institutions. We argue that in the post-Dobbs political climate, public support has shifted away from court-issued abortion decisions toward those made through voter referendums, driven by higher perceived procedural fairness in direct democracy. We fielded two unique survey experiments, one before the Dobbs decision removing the federal constitutional right for pregnant people to seek an abortion, and one after the decision. Pre-Dobbs, we find few differences in citizens’ perceptions of abortion decisions made by state courts, legislatures, or referendums. Post-Dobbs, we find that people evaluate both pro-abortion and anti-abortion decisions more favorably when decided through voter referendums. Our results hold critical implications for policies on abortion in the post-Dobbs landscape, but also for policy formation and evaluation on other contentious public policy issues.

title: “I Share Your Sentiment”—A Longitudinal Study of Facebook Post Sentiment and Sharing
abstract: This study examines how Norwegian political parties used negative, positive or neutral sentiment on Facebook over a 10-year period (2016–2025) and how such sentiment affected the sharing of their posts. Drawing on a full population of posts from all major parliamentary parties, the study investigates (a) whether negative sentiment increases over time, (b) how sentiment varies with party ideology and incumbency status, and (c) how positive and negative sentiment relate to sharing overall and at the party level. Demonstrating an approach using large language models in combination with human annotation for sentiment analysis, the study finds that while positive sentiment remains dominant, negative sentiment has increased over time, especially among challenger and left-wing parties. Extremist parties on both the far-left and far-right post more negative content, but this does not consistently translate into higher sharing. Overall, negative posts tend to receive more shares, but this advantage appears to weaken over time, suggesting strategic adaptation and possible audience fatigue.

title: The Fireside Database: Large-scale evidence from 25,419 psychedelic support interactions
authors: Felix Schoeller, Marc Santolini, Dana Xiadani, Mickael Eskinazi, Ashwin Murali, David Esselman, Wyatt Houtz, Wesley Bellanca, Joshua White
abstract: Most psychedelic experiences occur outside clinical settings, yet as policy frameworks rapidly expand to accommodate nonclinical use, no systematic data exist on who seeks psychedelic support, under what circumstances, or what makes that support effective. We present the Fireside Database, a US-based dataset comprising 25,419 peer support interactions conducted by 220 trained volunteers at Fireside Project’s Psychedelic Support Line between April 2021 and February 2026. The released resource integrates structured interaction logs with volunteer-coded metadata and 2777 caller satisfaction surveys across five outcome dimensions. Psilocybin was the most commonly reported substance (59.9% of coded interactions), while cannabis produced the highest distress rate (47.2%). The nested data structure—with 50 supporters each completing ≥10 surveyed interactions—supports multilevel modeling of individual supporter effects on caller outcomes. This resource enables research in psychedelic epidemiology, evidence-based training design, and the investigation of what makes psychedelic psychological support effective.
