title: Constructing an Elite: Identity and Boundary Work on a Darknet Drug Market
abstract: This article examines how users of Cebulka, the largest Polish-language darknet drug cryptomarket, construct and negotiate their online identities. Utilizing nineteen in-depth interviews with vendors and buyers, the research employs a qualitative methodology informed by reflexive thematic analysis, social identity theory, the SIDE model. Based on the data, five themes are developed: 1) lower perceived physical and social danger; 2) greater knowledge, technical competence, and access to higher-quality products; 3) care for others; 4) higher social status; and 5) separation between darknet personas and offline lives. Across these themes, Cebulka’s users collectively framed themselves as an elite community distinct from street-level market participants. Thus the cryptomarket operates not just as a transactional space but as a site of identity work and symbolic boundary drawing—one that inverts the context collapse and algorithmic datafication typical of the visible web. These findings carry implications for harm reduction, drug policy, and the sociology of online communities, while highlighting the ambivalent, exclusionary character of the market’s technical barriers.

title: On the Uses of “Queer” in Demography
authors: Christopher Julian, Christina Pao, D'Lane Compton
abstract: The phrase “queer demography” appears in conference sessions, scholarly groups, and peer-reviewed journal articles. Critically engaging with terminology matters as the field unfolds. Drawing on precedents from family studies, we map, rather than fix, how “queer” is used in relation to “demography”: queer as a noun (the demography of queer populations); queer as an adjective (demography merged with queer epistemology); and queer as a verb (to queer demography). Rather than settling on a definition of “queer,” we take its resistance to definition and its commitment to unsettling identity categories seriously, reading these uses against demography’s legacy of enumeration and classification and alongside other critical orientations to population studies. We invite those in and outside the field to reflect on what is gained and lost when “queer” is attached to “demography,” and on how current discourse might keep the subfield’s meaning open rather than settled.

title: Contingent Democrats: Electoral Accountability and Democratic Commitments in an Electoral Autocracy
abstract: How do voters interpret electoral outcomes and reassess democracy when elections take place in electoral autocracies? We examine these questions using a preregistered two-wave panel of 1,157 respondents surrounding Hungary's 2026 election, which ended Viktor Orbán's sixteen-year rule. We find asymmetric patterns of electoral accountability: opposition supporters attribute defeat partly to their own parties' shortcomings but primarily explain victory through incumbent failures, while incumbent supporters largely deflect responsibility for defeat. Consistent with the winner-loser gap, victorious opposition supporters evaluate democratic quality and electoral integrity more positively, while defeated incumbent supporters become more skeptical. Electoral turnover also reshapes support for democratic constraints. Incumbent supporters become more supportive of several constraints after defeat, while exploratory analyses suggest that opposition supporters with initially strong democratic commitments become somewhat more tolerant of institutional restrictions after victory. These findings suggest that voters' interpretations of electoral outcomes and support for democratic institutions may depend partly on their relationship to political power.

title: Schools and Learning Inequality: A Theoretical Model and Quasi-Experimental Evidence
abstract: Do schools reduce or amplify learning gaps by socioeconomic background? I develop a formal model that clarifies the estimands implicit in the literature and synthesizes its seemingly contradictory findings by distinguishing between exposure, or how much schooling children receive, and quality, or which schools they attend. The model shows that schools can compensate for inequality, by displacing more unequal learning outside school, while simultaneously reproducing it, both positionally, through the sorting of children into schools of unequal quality, and dispositionally, through differences in how children convert schooling into learning. Empirically, I test three of the model's predictions using Danish register data and variation from changes in school district boundaries over time. I find that the effects of school quality exceed those of exposure, are concentrated among socioeconomically disadvantaged children, and are larger where sorting into schools is stronger. Equalizing school quality can therefore be an effective means of reducing learning inequalities.

title: Asymmetric Warfare and Implications for Counter-Terrorism Operations in North-East Nigeria
abstract: This study examined asymmetric warfare and its implications for counter-terrorism operations in North-East Nigeria. The study was motivated by the persistence of Boko Haram and Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) despite sustained military operations and the resulting need to understand why conventional superiority has not translated into decisive and sustainable security outcomes. The study adopted a qualitative literature review design based on peer-reviewed journal articles, scholarly books and chapters, Nigerian policy documents, and relevant institutional and regional security materials. The analysis was organised around three issues: the characteristics of asymmetric warfare in North-East Nigeria, its implications for counter-terrorism operations, and its consequences for national security policy. The study was anchored on Asymmetry Theory and Securitization Theory. The analysis indicates that the principal advantage of insurgent groups does not derive from superior firepower but from their ability to exploit differences in political objectives, operational flexibility, mobility, local knowledge, civilian environments and the costs associated with prolonged conflict. The literature also indicates that Nigeria’s counter-terrorism response has achieved operational successes but continues to encounter difficulties associated with intelligence integration, inter-agency coordination, civilian protection, socio-economic vulnerability and cross-border insurgent mobility. The study further finds that the securitization of terrorism has facilitated the mobilisation of extraordinary security resources, but threat framing alone does not resolve the institutional and developmental conditions that sustain insecurity. The study argues that effective counter-terrorism requires an integrated approach in which military operations are complemented by intelligence coordination, community-based security, regional cooperation, civilian protection, institutional strengthening and measures addressing socio-economic vulnerability. The article concludes that the central policy challenge is not the absence of military capacity alone but the difficulty of converting security capacity into sustained institutional and human security outcomes.

title: Measuring four dimensions of climate change skepticism: The CCS-4 scale
abstract: Despite overwhelming evidence of climate change, a significant portion of the population remains skeptical. Because existing instruments fail to capture the full spectrum of skepticism (trend, attribution, impact, and response) we integrated and refined scales originally developed by Whitmarsh (2011) and De Graaf et al. (2023) to the newly proposed, four-dimensional CCS-4 scale. For initial scale development, we utilized an online panel and employed confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) to evaluate the instrument's dimensionality, scalability, and reliability. We propose both a short (8-item) and a long (12-item) version of the CCS-4 scale. We then validate the scales using two waves of the large-scale, population representative, probability-based GLEN survey (n=16,226/2,060). The resulting scale correlates significantly with established predictors of skepticism and is available in both German and English for future research.

title: Living With Canids in Wisconsin — Mapping the Currencies of the Wolf Conflict
abstract: Wisconsin’s conflict over our relationship with the wolf is argued where populations are counted and status is set in law. The middle ground between them — where a person comes to believe what he believes about relationship together with others (psychological and social identity) — is nearly empty in the public record. In four sections this paper treats the conflict over wolves as historical, structural and systemic and offers a scaffold and a method for locating any response to it, based upon the scientific literature and evidence-based programmatic efforts. Procuring a Life describes the declining and recovering population records of four predator and four prey animals — beaver, bison, elk, deer, dog, fox, coyote, wolf — in the terms of the currencies into which each was placed by those who effectively exerted control over what happened to those populations. Processing into Provision or Product defines a currency as the form into which an animal’s life is converted — food and clothing, fur, money, symbol and knowledge — and then follows the animal through nine conversions by human hands. From provision to sign, the passage of one skin, a mink coat, is followed through every hand that held it. Causes and Consequences of Conversion names the four hands at every conversion — producer, promoter, arbitrator, processor of currency and value— and finds four regularities in the passage: value rises with each hand; distance from the source and repeated conversion in form increasingly disconnects the handler from relationship with the animal; cost and benefit accrue unequally; and return to original sources has no reliable mechanism of its own. This accounting is contrasted with the value the living wolf produces that no hand holds: fewer deer–vehicle collisions and a richer understory, absent from the conflict because few keep an accounting of them. Mapping Layers characterizes five relevant systemic levels, and finds the critical two middle layers — psycho-social identity development and small-group formation — without survey, study or program. In the one Washburn County district followed class by class, the boys stand above the state in language at grade 8 and at the state at grade 11 — the years in which hunting is learned — a loss the structure of the households does not predict and the paper reads as made in the sparse-language groups, the team and then the camp, whose standards a few leaders set. The review of the literature distinguishes the ecologists’ attitude surveys from a developmental psychologist’s study of motivation still to be done, compares a scaffold of women’s intergenerational return of relationship beside the market chain that skims off value at each phase of conversion, and closes with PACKS, a five-year family-based research methodology and program designed to fill the gap in conceiving ways to resolve our conflicts around wolves and other wild animals.

title: Conservation volunteering and its link to nature connection, wellbeing and pro-environmental behaviours in Australia
authors: Usitha Rajeevan, Emily Flies, Pauline Marsh, Brenda Lin
abstract: Human nature connectedness (HNC), the relationship between humans and non-human nature, can benefit wellbeing and pro-environmental behaviours (PEBs). However, research on HNC and PEBs have mostly explored private sphere behaviours, such as consumption choices, while public sphere behaviours, such as volunteering for conservation, remain relatively understudied. In this study we gathered data from 135 conservation volunteers in Australia through an online survey that captured quantitative and qualitative information pertaining to their HNC, wellbeing, PEBs and motivations for volunteering. We found that conservation volunteers have higher HNC, life satisfaction and PEB scores compared to the general population. Positive associations occurred between HNC and PEBs and between HNC and ecocentric worldviews. Qualitative responses showed that multiple wellbeing aspects were both drivers and outcomes of conservation volunteering and that underlying values and volunteering positively influence engagement in PEBs. These findings can support conservation organisations in recruiting and achieving positive outcomes for volunteers and environments.

title: Wonder, Meaning and Action: Stories of Nature Connection, Wellbeing and Environmentalism in Australia
authors: Usitha Rajeevan, Emily Flies, Pauline Marsh, Brenda Lin
abstract: 1. Human nature connectedness (HNC) positively impacts human wellbeing and pro-environmental behaviours and is a leverage point for improving environmental outcomes. To date, most studies on HNC focus either on the wellbeing impacts or environmental outcomes of HNC, missing potential interlinkages between these three concepts and limiting our understanding of impacts resulting from the intersections. 2. To explore the meanings of these intersections we analysed 30 stories of HNC told by people living in Australia in which nature connection, wellbeing and environmentalism (PEBs and attitudes) intersected. It was found there is generally a positive relationship among the three concepts, with the exception that exposure to environmental destruction triggered negative emotions. Four themes were generated to describe the commonalities at the intersection: 1) Enthralled by nature 2) A lifetime of connection to nature 3) Reciprocity with nature and 4) Greater-than-self. 3. These stories where HNC intersects with wellbeing and PEBs, often described finding awe, beauty, wonder or magic in nature suggesting it being vital for a deeper connection to nature. The stories demonstrate that HNC, which often starts with a strong childhood connection to nature, can be maintained throughout life via multiple nature experiences. Further, they show how being in a reciprocal relationship with nature helps the wellbeing of both people and nature. Additionally, a focus beyond the individual self, an interest in the greater good for humanity or nature, was expressed in these stories. 4. With regards to HNC dimensions, we found that although a strong emotional connection to nature was associated with pro-environmental actions, people sometimes felt negative effects on their emotional wellbeing due to it. All the other dimensions of HNC were positively associated with both wellbeing and positive environmental outcomes. 5. Policy implications: Supporting lifelong nature connection through health and environmental policies can result in positive impacts for human and environmental wellbeing. However, attempts to restore people’s broken relationship with nature must take care to support wellbeing in the context of environmental destruction and degradation. Findings suggest that conservation volunteering, gardening and hunting are activities that synergistically support HNC, and human and environmental wellbeing.

title: Trump’s Second Presidency: A Public Perspective
abstract: Donald Trump’s second presidency has generated intense controversy among policymakers, investors, and the public. Existing research has largely examined specific policies or measured public opinion through surveys distinguishing support from opposition. Using Google Trends data from January 2025 to September 2026, this study examines the drivers of public attention to Trump, associated political narratives, and cross-national spillover. First, attention peaks are associated with major political events and policy developments, including executive actions, immigration, government restructuring, trade disputes, social policies, and international conflicts. Second, opposition-oriented narratives exhibit a more consistent relation with overall attention to Trump than supporter-oriented narratives, such as Make America Great Again, America First, and religiously framed support, whose associations vary across political circumstances. Third, there are different patterns of political attention spillover. In Australia, Trump-related attention has a stronger and more persistent predictive relation with Pauline Hanson than with Anthony Albanese. In the United Kingdom, the corresponding relations with Nigel Farage and Keir Starmer are broadly similar, although their lag structures differ. These findings suggest that political attention spillovers depend on both ideological affinity and domestic political and diplomatic contexts. This study offers a novel framework for examining public attention beyond conventional measures of political approval and provides a foundation for future research on public narratives, policy preferences, and government decision-making.

title: Active Recovery Is Not Just for Athletes: Employees Need to Train for Recovery to Enhance Work
abstract: Trials of recovery training report mean gains in psychological detachment, but the mean does not show whether training helped the employees who detached least or those who already detached well. An aptitude-treatment account predicts larger gains at the low end of the baseline distribution (compensation), and a cumulative-advantage account predicts larger gains at the high end (accumulation). I tested the two accounts in a prespecified reanalysis of a randomized trial among German employees (N = 393, 76% women, mean age 41; 247 with posttest data) that compared a wait-list control with a 6-week cognitive-behavioral recovery training and a 6-week mindfulness-based training. The primary test was the baseline × condition interaction in a Lin-adjusted regression of posttest detachment; secondary analyses were quantile treatment effects, changes-in-changes and Lee bounds, multiple imputation, and a missingness model. Both trainings raised detachment at the mean baseline by about 0.9 points, and quantile effects were larger at the .25 than at the .75 quantile in both groups. The cognitive-behavioral interaction was −0.21 (95% CI [−0.50, 0.08]), leaning toward compensation, and the mindfulness interaction 0.04 (95% CI [−0.24, 0.33]); the condition contrast was 0.25 (95% CI [−0.01, 0.51]), and all three intervals included zero. Dropout before the posttest was not detectably patterned by baseline detachment in any group. The results support neither compensation nor accumulation. Neither training detectably favored employees at either end of the baseline distribution, and the intervals bound how large either pattern could be in a trial of this size.

title: Synthetic Reception: Manufacturing the Signals of Uptake in Hype and Technology Expectations
abstract: Hype is made in its reception as well as in its promises. Audiences decide what deserves attention partly by observing one another, and counts, first reactions and endorsements tell each observer what others find worth engaging with. Research on hype and expectations reads these signals of uptake as organic, as the sum of independent judgements. I systematise reception as a focus for this research and propose synthetic reception: a producer’s concealed contribution to a signal of uptake that observers read as given off by independent audience members. What it fakes is the independence of the signal. The concept draws on research on hype, signalling and trust, starts from a music-marketing agency’s account of its own methods, and reaches into science (paper mills) and technology (a reported creator campaign). Four facets target the inferences audiences draw from the uptake of others: how many attend (momentum), what the uptake says (vox populi), whether someone with standing has judged it (authority) and whether it is the participants’ own (authenticity). Each corresponds to an object of hype research, from attention curves to the appropriation of circulating representations and sociotechnical imaginaries. For technology assessment, the concept adds a question to its reading of public uptake as a signal of relevance: whether that uptake is organic.

title: The Role of Traditional Conflict Resolution Mechanisms in Local Peacebuilding in Auchi, Edo State, Nigeria: A Qualitative Case Study
authors: Salihu Musa Haruna, Cyrille Ngamen Kouassi
abstract: Traditional conflict resolution remains an important component of local peace governance in many Nigerian communities, yet its contemporary operation cannot be understood solely through claims of cultural legitimacy or accessibility. This study examines how the Otaru-in-Council functions as a local peacebuilding institution in Auchi, Edo State, with attention to its mechanisms, perceived contributions, inclusionary limits and interaction with formal justice institutions. The study examines the structure and functions of the Otaru-in-Council, identifies the conflict resolution mechanisms employed, assesses their perceived advantages and challenges, and considers conditions for constructive interaction between traditional and formal justice systems. A qualitative case study design was adopted. Primary evidence was obtained through in-depth semi-structured interviews with 30 purposively selected participants comprising traditional rulers and palace officials, senior chiefs and elders, ward and quarter heads, youth representatives, women representatives, civil society actors and community residents. Two non-participant observations of open dispute-resolution sessions and documentary materials supplemented the interviews. Data were analysed thematically, with triangulation, member checking and thick description used to strengthen trustworthiness. Mediation, reconciliation rituals, adjudication, consensus-building and arbitration were reported as principal mechanisms. Participants associated the traditional institution with cultural legitimacy, relatively low cost, accessibility, speed and restoration of social relations. At the same time, respondents reported gender exclusion, weak documentation, political interference, elite bias, limited enforcement capacity and tensions with formal law. The findings suggest that the contribution of the Otaru-in-Council to local peacebuilding is conditioned by both legitimacy and institutional safeguards. The Otaru-in-Council should be understood neither as a substitute for the state justice system nor as an inherently effective institution. Its peacebuilding significance lies in its embeddedness in local social relations and its capacity to convene disputants, while its limitations arise partly from exclusion, politicisation and uncertain interfaces with formal law. Reforms should clarify referral and jurisdictional boundaries, strengthen documentation, widen women’s and youth participation, develop human-rights and procedural capacity, and establish practical coordination between customary and formal institutions without eroding the authority that makes local mechanisms socially meaningful.

title: Regional firefighter communications networks in Los Angeles County: A perspective-based analysis
abstract: Emergency responder communications failures have long posed challenges to interagency coordination, prompting nationwide efforts to improve interoperability following the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks. However, the extent to which regional initiatives have addressed persistent communications barriers remains an important question. This study evaluates the efficacy of regional firefighter communications systems in Los Angeles County, California, focusing on the Los Angeles Regional Interoperable Communications System (LARICS) and the Interagency Communications Interoperability System (ICI). Its purpose is to examine how these initiatives support interdepartmental coordination and identify what limitations, experienced during 9/11, continue into the present day. The study employed a two-phase qualitative approach grounded in first responder perspectives. Phase I consisted of open-ended interviews with four personnel across three Los Angeles County fire departments, including two field personnel and two communications personnel. Phase II used a five-point Likert scale to assess participants’ perceptions of communications technology, its development over their careers, and the relative influence of technological and procedural factors on communications challenges. Findings indicate that regional interoperability initiatives have supported interdepartmental coordination and provided redundant communications channels. Interviewees generally reported improvements in communications technology over their careers and satisfaction with existing systems, while also identifying continuing needs for improvement. Persistent barriers include radio signal attenuation inside buildings, incompatible technologies and frequencies, and differences in agency terminology and procedures. Participants did not consistently attribute communications problems primarily to technological limitations, underscoring the importance of organizational practices alongside equipment. Although the small, nonrandom interview sample limits generalizability, the findings suggest that regional initiatives have improved communications capabilities without fully resolving the operational challenges facing firefighters.

title: Functional Relocation of Authority in Decentralization: Institutional Change and Local Government Autonomy in Punjab, Pakistan
abstract: Decentralization is expected to strengthen local democracy, yet Punjab’s local governments have operated with limited administrative and fiscal autonomy despite repeated reforms since 2001. Documentary thematic analysis, structured around a mechanism-based framework, traces institutional provisions in legislation, amendments, consultation reports, and audit records for 2001–2022. Authority has been repeatedly relocated across provincially controlled offices and bodies rather than transferred to elected institutions, termed functional relocation of authority. The Deputy Commissioner, a colonial-era district office within Pakistan’s elite civil service cadres, exemplifies this: its coordinating role was relocated to the Chief Officer under the 2013 reform before being reintroduced by name in 2019, showing that the underlying function, not any single office, persists. Four pathways operationalize it: administrative authority concentration, fiscal oversight, functional displacement, and institutional reversibility. These mechanisms reproduce institutional dependency and constrain elected local governments’ autonomy, offering a structural account of persistent local-government ineffectiveness in Punjab’s decentralization framework.

title: Social Contacts of Older People in 27 European Countries. The Role of Welfare Spending and Economic Inequality
authors: Lea Ellwardt, Sascha, Patrick Präg, Nardi Steverink
abstract: Social contacts of older people have consistently been associated with good health and longevity. The extent of individual social contacts, however, varies considerably between countries. We study why countries differ in amounts of social contacts of older adults. Using theory on income inequality and neo-materialism, we expect the amount of social contacts of older people to be highest in countries with low income inequality and comprehensive welfare spending. Furthermore, we hypothesize that the impact of country characteristics on social contacts differs with individual income and age. We combine individual-level data from the European Social Survey with country-level data from Eurostat, and test two dimensions of social contacts of people aged ≥60 years: having a close contact and meeting socially. Cross-national comparison of 27 European countries is realized through linear and logistic multilevel modeling. The results reveal partial support for our expectations. Income inequality and old-age poverty reduce the likelihood of having a close contact. Welfare spending, specifically expenditure on care for older adults and health services, has the potential to cancel out some of these negative effects. However, there were only small differences between age groups. The implications of these findings are being discussed.

title: Fossil AI and the Making of Powered Land in Texas
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure is driving a historic convergence of digital and energy capital. Examining Stargate Abilene and gas-linked data centers across Texas, we show how ostensibly liberalized electricity markets and state coordination make computational development investable. This produces “powered land,” as energy access and development rights are assembled and repeatedly reworked around speculative demand for compute. We theorize “Fossil AI” as a mode of accumulation in which state institutions intertwine with the inherited hydrocarbon economy to revalorize fossil infrastructure. Appeals to grid “reliability” translate private requirements into matters of public planning and system security amid geopolitical competition over AI.

title: Tracing the Emergence of "Queer Demography"
abstract: “Queer demography” is here—but when did it emerge, and what even is it? Despite the term striking sexualities scholars as oxymoronic, it is now being used by some researchers, indicating new possibilities for demography and possible shifts within the knowledge cultures of sexualities scholarship more broadly. To trace the emergence and circulation of “queer demography,” I conducted quantitative and qualitative content analyses of two corpora that capture the heart of the field: all articles ever published on relevant topics in Demography (n=59), the flagship journal of the Population Association of America (PAA), and all program listings on relevant topics appearing in the last decade of PAA’s annual meetings (n=416). I investigate how the field uses this language, the context for its emergence, and what meaningful work it might be doing. I argue that the arrival of “queer demography” is a critical culmination but also a juncture, and that its meaning and usefulness remains unsettled. In tracing its historical emergence and contemporary proliferation out of a broader long-running background of LGBT-inclusive demographic work, I argue that scholars must understand this genealogy as the backdrop that produces a wide range of quantified sexuality knowledge. My project is both a critique and a celebration: my goal is to assess what it is possible for demography to know about sexuality, and what might still be possible to learn in the future.

title: Making Randomized Controlled Trials Culturally Responsive: A Practical Framework
authors: Fatima Tuz Zahra, Ayesha S. Boyce
abstract: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are widely used to establish causal effects, yet conventional procedures may overlook cultural contexts that shape participation, measurement, and research outcomes. This article introduces Culturally Responsive Randomized Controlled Trials (CRRCTs), a practical framework for integrating cultural responsiveness into RCT design and implementation without compromising methodological rigor. Drawing on existing literature and illustrative cases, the article presents the 4Rs Framework—Reflection, Reciprocity, Reach, and Relevance—and a 10-step workflow to guide culturally responsive practices throughout the trial lifecycle. The framework links these practices to established risks of bias, including selection, attrition, detection, reporting, and interference. By embedding community engagement, culturally valid measurement, equitable participation, and accessible dissemination into trial procedures, CRRCTs position cultural responsiveness as an essential component of research validity rather than an optional addition.

title: Wealth and Childbearing: how economic resources shape reproductive transitions in Italy
authors: Gianluca Truscello, Daniela Bellani, Maria Chiara Zanarotti
abstract: Research on the economic determinants of fertility has mainly focused on current household’s and individual’s resources such as income and employment, while household wealth has received comparatively less attention. Unlike income, wealth reflects a stock of resources accumulated over time and may therefore capture a more durable dimension of economic security, providing a buffer against income losses, unexpected expenses, and future economic shocks. This paper examines whether household wealth is associated with subsequent childbearing in Italy, distinguishing between different wealth measures. Using longitudinal SHIW data for 1995-2022, collected by the Bank of Italy, we estimate random-effects logit models examining the associations of gross wealth, net worth, and debt with childbearing transitions among heterosexual couples. Despite the theoretical expectation of a positive association, we find little evidence that greater accumulated wealth increases the probability of childbearing. Interaction analyses further suggest that accumulated wealth may acquire greater relevance within specific socioeconomic and partnership contexts. Overall, our findings do not support a general positive wealth-childbearing relationship, while pointing to possible heterogeneity across partnership and socioeconomic groups.

title: Tenability: A Name, a Test, and Seven Drafting Devices for Procedures That Do Not Have to Be Broken
abstract: Formalization is necessary to operation and is the standard remedy after coordination failure: when an event goes badly, the response is almost always more specification. This paper argues that the remedy routinely produces the defect it was meant to cure, because a procedure specified tightly enough to remove discretion cannot be followed in the conditions for which it was most needed. The cost is not the single departure but the standing the instrument loses once it is known to require breaking. A formal structure is tenable when it can be complied with as written across the conditions it governs, including conditions it did not anticipate, without anyone having to breach or override it. Tenability is distinct from flexibility, vagueness, and permissiveness, and is achieved by restricting what an instrument claims rather than by adding to it. Seven drafting devices accomplish that restriction: scope restriction, tiered normativity, anchored discretion, burden allocation, precedence rules, guidance by worked example, and temporal and successional scoping. The paper treats these as alternative routes to one property rather than a checklist, illustrated from statute, case law, and municipal and federal practice, including a 2025 decision voiding a municipal agreement drafted so that it had to be broken. The contribution is conceptual: a name, a diagnostic test applicable to any existing instrument, a repair inventory pairing each device with the failure it forestalls, and a reframing of policy review from what an instrument omits to what can no longer be followed. Existing work names the tension between rules and practice but takes the drafting as given.

title: Is Ukraine to Blame for Rising Diesel Prices in the US? A Test of the Trump Thesis
abstract: In October 2026, US President Donald Trump blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for the rising price of diesel in the United States. Using event study methodologies and parametric and non-parametric testing, we examine this thesis. Our results show that Ukrainian strikes had a minor negative effect on oil prices across three different fuel oils. On the other hand, geopolitical events connected with the US war on Iran, and in particular Iranian strikes on Gulf oil infrastructure and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, were highly significantly correlated with much higher prices.

title: Techno-nationalism and Huawei’s Technological Rise
authors: Ran JIAO, Hanxi GUO, Yuxin PENG
abstract: As technological competition between China and the United States intensifies, Huawei’s development has become a key case study for examining Chinese techno-nationalism. The launch of Huawei’s Mate 60 series has made it a symbol of breakthroughs in advanced semiconductor technology. Treating this event as a significant milestone in Huawei’s technological innovation, this paper asks: How has techno-nationalism manifested in Huawei’s development following the imposition of sanctions against the company, against the backdrop of U.S.-China technological competition? This paper argues that this event was not merely a corporate product launch or an act of market competition, but also a concentrated manifestation of the interaction between national strategy and corporate policies within the context of Chinese techno-nationalism.

title: VOICE, POWER, AND AGENTIC AI: WOMEN’S STRATEGIC AGENCY IN IDENTITY-DIVERSE DECISION ENVIRONMENTS IN THE GLOBAL SOUTH
abstract: Generative and agentic artificial intelligence are reshaping strategic decision-making, but their empowering effects depend on how participation, leadership, technological capability, hierarchy, and algorithmic legitimacy interact. Drawing on Sociotechnical Systems Theory and Psychological Empowerment Theory, this study tests a moderated-mediation model using survey data from 376 women in decision-involved roles in Pakistan and PLS-SEM. Women’s Engagement in Decision-Making, Inclusive Leadership, and Generative AI Capability positively predict Perceived Enterprise Use of Agentic AI Capabilities (PEAIC), which in turn increases Psychological Empowerment and mediates all three relationships. Power Distance Orientation weakens the three antecedent–PEAIC links, whereas Perceived Algorithmic Fairness strengthens the PEAIC–empowerment relationship. The findings show that human-centric AI transformation depends not only on technical capability but also on voice, authority, and perceived fairness in identity-diverse Global South workplaces.

title: Digital Spillovers and Regional Growth in the European Union: Spatial Panel Econometrics with Machine-Learning Clustering and Validation for 234 NUTS-2 Regions, 2017–2024
authors: Ada Spiru, Maria Buonarota, Carlo Drago, Alberto Costantiello, Angelo Leogrande
abstract: Does digital adoption raise regional prosperity in the region where it occurs, or does it work through neighbouring regions? We assemble a georeferenced panel of 234 EU NUTS-2 regions observed from 2017 to 2024, linking Eurostat data on GDP per capita in purchasing power standards, household broadband and internet use, employment and social exclusion to NUTS 2024 boundaries. Global Moran's I is positive and significant for every variable and year (0.39–0.78), and LISA maps reveal persistent high-income and low-income clusters. Non-spatial estimators give a positive digital coefficient: 0.21% higher GDP per capita per percentage point of adoption under two-way fixed effects, and 1.83% when lagged adoption instruments a noisy, survey-based regressor. However, fixed-effects residuals remain spatially autocorrelated, and a Spatial Durbin Model (ρ = 0.70) shows that the own-region (direct) effect is not significant, while the spillover (indirect) effect is positive (0.20% per point, p = 0.039) and robust across three spatial weight matrices. Of six clustering algorithms compared on eleven validity indices, Ward hierarchical clustering performs best and identifies seven spatially contiguous regional profiles. Of six machine-learning regressors, a random forest validated by region-grouped cross-validation performs best (out-of-sample R² = 0.57). Its SHAP decomposition reproduces the econometric signs: own adoption dominates in levels, while neighbours' adoption and employment dominate within regions. Digital policy in the EU should therefore be targeted at the level of functional macro-regions, not individual regions.

title: Menopausal Hormone Therapy in the Netherlands: Prevalence, Use Patterns, User Experiences, and Reasons for Use and Non-Use
authors: Marijke Schotanus-Dijkstra, Laura Huiberts, Constance H.C. Drossaert, Franciska de Beer, Judith Veld, Laura Weiss, Rosa Boeschoten, Marianne Simons, Astrid Kamperman
abstract: Background: Menopausal Hormone Therapy (MHT) has received renewed clinical and public attention but population-based prevalence estimates and detailed information on women’s experiences with MHT remain limited. This study examined the prevalence and socio-demographic and reproductive characteristics of MHT use among Dutch women aged 40-60 years as well as patterns of use, user experiences, and reasons for use and non-use. Methods: Data for population-based prevalence estimates were obtained from the Dutch Longitudinal Internet Studies for the Social Sciences (LISS) in 2024 (n = 924) and 2025 (n = 775), and data on MHT use patterns and user experiences were obtained from a convenience sample collected in 2026 (n = 1,653). Results: Estimated MHT prevalence increased from 5.1% in 2024 to 6.5% in 2025 and married participants were less likely to use MHT than non-married participants. The convenience sample showed that most users reported positive experiences with MHT and substantial improvements in sleep problems, irritability, exhaustion and depressive mood. Nevertheless, many women reported difficulties obtaining adequate information about MHT, optimizing their dosage, and having to consult multiple healthcare professionals before receiving appropriate care. Among non-users, preferences for non-hormonal approaches, concerns about side effects and health risks, and limited knowledge about MHT were common reasons for not considering treatment. Conclusions: MHT use in the Netherlands is increasing but remains relatively uncommon. Users appear to seek and experience benefits from MHT that extend beyond vasomotor symptoms, highlighting the need for longitudinal research on symptom trajectories and treatment outcomes across the menopausal transition.

title: Who Pays, Who Benefits? Housing Inequalities and the Ecological Transition in France, Tested with Stakeholders Report on the ReHousIn Policy Lab #2
authors: Tommaso Vitale, Federica Rotondo, Marco Cremaschi, Sarah Bouchafa
abstract: his report documents the second ReHousIn Policy Lab for France, an open public seminar held in Paris on 25 September 2026 to test, rather than validate, the project’s intermediate findings on how green transition policies shape housing inequalities. The research team presented the comparative work on nine European countries and 27 cases, together with the French findings drawn from four neighbourhood case studies (Orgues de Flandre and Clichy-Batignolles in Paris, Argonne in Orléans, Champs-Plaisants in Sens) and three scenario workshops. The interpretive frame treats tenure status as a distributive filter and examines multilevel governance and territorial filtering across three policy families: energy retrofit, densification and nature-based solutions. Five housing experts from Apur, the Fondation pour le Logement des Défavorisés, AORIF, OFCE and the École urbaine of Sciences Po responded, followed by testimony from tenants. The transcribed discussion was analysed by theme and stakeholder group, and each intervention was tagged as confirming, nuancing, contesting or adding to the findings. Positions converged on three orientations: articulating climate and housing policy with stable public funding, capturing part of the land value created by public investment, and treating social housing as an infrastructure with the means to invest. They partly converged on targeting retrofit aid at modest households and on strengthening local engineering capacity, and diverged on easing pressure on Paris through territorial planning. At the European level, the lessons concern implementation rather than instruments: the same instruments produce different effects depending on tenure structures, financing arrangements, land control and local capacities. This report documents the second ReHousIn Policy Lab (Paris, 25 September 2026), where findings from four French neighbourhood case studies and a nine-country comparison were tested against the views of Apur, the Fondation pour le Logement des Défavorisés, AORIF, OFCE, the École urbaine and tenants. Participants converged on three priorities: linking climate and housing policy with stable funding, capturing the land value created by public investment, and treating social housing as infrastructure. They disagreed on how to target retrofit aid and on how to ease pressure on Paris.

title: ChatGPT Access and Writing Skill: A Bayesian Reanalysis of an Online Randomized Experiment
abstract: Generative writing tools are entering professional work, and their effects differ across people. I reanalyze a published online randomized experiment in which college-educated professionals in six writing-intensive occupations completed two incentivized writing tasks, and a randomly assigned half were given access to ChatGPT before the second task (Noy & Zhang, 2023a). I ask whether access weakens the link between first-task and second-task writing grades, whether that weakening is stronger for writing than for content, whether access narrows differences between people more for originality than for writing quality, and how access relates to felt effectiveness and enjoyment on the task. Grades and ratings are standardized; the analysis plan, fixed beforehand, retests hypotheses already tested on these data. Bayesian regression models with weakly informative priors are fit to the linear and convex incentive conditions. Each estimate is a posterior median with a 95% equal-tailed credible interval and the posterior probability of the predicted direction, P(direction), with no decision cutoffs. Under access, second-task writing grades depended less on first-task grades, −0.159 [−0.317, −0.002], with P(direction) = .976; the data did not distinguish content from writing interactions, or originality from writing spread ratios. Access was associated with higher enjoyment (0.44 [0.29, 0.60]); felt effectiveness was 0.12 [−0.06, 0.29], P(direction) = .905. After a disclosed code correction, two-month workplace use of ChatGPT, the secondary outcome, was 13.4 [3.0, 23.5] percentage points higher under access. For organizations, results suggest one structured encounter was associated with higher enjoyment and followed by more use at work.

title: Presuming or Building Capacity? Contractualisation, Matrices of Agency and the Position of Recipients in Local Welfare
abstract: This paper compares two sociomedical rehabilitation devices based on cash transfers, introduced in Italy under Law 328/2000, the voucher of Lombardy and the care budget of Local Health Authority Caserta 2 in Campania, and shows that in local welfare the same contractual form places recipients in opposite positions depending on the regulatory role of local public administration. Drawing on the sociology of policy instruments and on the economies of worth, it treats agency as a conventional criterion of evaluation and distinguishes four matrices of agency, market, domestic, civic and projective, each giving activation and contractualisation a different meaning. The voucher presumes the capacity to choose, grants exit without voice and lets providers turn away difficult cases, so it works for recipients who already have autonomy or family support. The care budget treats capacity as the goal of intervention and keeps a public third party inside an incomplete, continuously renegotiated contract. Administrative responsibility by process is the mechanism behind the difference; without a floor of enforceable rights, it slides into discretion and personal dependence. A postscript reads four later forms of contractualisation through the matrices: conditionality pacts in minimum income schemes, payment by results, personal and health budgets, and the coprogramming of services with the third sector. Whether a contract presumes or builds the capacity of recipients depends on three conditions: capacity treated as goal rather than premise, a public third party inside the contract, and a floor of rights beyond negotiation. The argument applies to recipients with low levels of autonomy in regionalised welfare systems.

title: Religion, Science, Government, Economics, and Humanitarian Progress Scores in 100 Countries and 50 US States
abstract: Previous research found that religious commitment is associated with poorer health outcomes, including neglect of science-based policies for disease and injury prevention, acquiescence in or support for autocratic government, and disdain for scientists whose research calls religious dogma into question. This study uses Social Progress Index scores for 100 populous countries and 50 US states to examine their association with religious commitment, controlling statistically for income and democratic government. Multiple regression analysis was used to estimate how much daily prayer frequency, income relative to the cost of living, and the degree of democratic governance predict Social Progress Index scores. In both studies, higher prayer frequency strongly predicted lower social progress. Higher per capita incomes, adjusted for the cost of living, and higher democracy scores were associated with higher social progress scores. Together, these three factors predicted an extraordinary share of the variation in the recent status of humanitarian progress.

title: A utility-based framework for evaluating the distributive effects of public transport projects on perceived accessibility
authors: Matheus Fontenelle Siqueira, Carlos Felipe Grangeiro Loureiro
abstract: Cost-benefit analysis, largely applied in transport appraisal, is criticized as utilitarian because it sums monetized gains across groups, but not because it uses utility as information. Yet the utility-based accessibility measure, the logsum of a discrete choice model, has been kept at the margin of equity analysis on the assumption that it carries the same commitment. Drawing on Sen's distinction between welfarism and sum-ranking and on the capability approach, this paper argues that a logsum of perceived accessibility can inform distinct distributive principles, provided it is expressed in units that remove its arbitrary level and model-specific scale, and proposes such a unit, job equivalents. The measure is applied to the ex-post evaluation of the metro and light rail lines of Fortaleza, Brazil, for low-income workers, with a destination-mode logsum estimated from stated and revealed preference data, segmented by gender and income and conditioned on the modes each person can use; census data show that the lines did not detectably change land use around the stations. In the case study, in job equivalents the lowest-income strata gain most, whereas in money higher-income men do, a reversal explained by modal preferences and by the weight of impedance in destination choice; the benefit concentrates along the corridors and bypasses the poorest periphery; and assuming universal mode availability understates the benefit to captive transit users two- to threefold. A structural equation model on the household travel survey shows that the benefit converts only partially into rail use, as expected, accounting for about seven percent of the association between proximity to the stations and use; the rest runs through channels outside the transport benefit as measured, such as residential self-selection, crowding on the trains and the lack of fare integration.

title: Does AI transcribe every accent as General American? Variety normalization in phonetic transcription by multimodal models
authors: Felipe de Paula Marques, Cândido Oliveira
abstract: Multimodal language models transcribe speech phonetically and are already proposed for pronunciation teaching, with the transcription treated as a neutral record of the signal. This study tests whether such a model preserves the variation between speakers or moves it toward General American (GA). Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite transcribed 117 Speech Accent Archive speakers in five prestige tiers, three times each, under a standard and an anticitation instruction, and the study compared each output with the archive's expert IPA. The model's transcriptions of different speakers were separated by about a fifth of the distance between the expert's transcriptions of the same speakers (convergence ratio 0.20, 95% CI [0.18, 0.22]), by a similar factor in every tier, and lay closer than the expert's to a GA reference and, above all, to the citation forms of isolated words, with American rhoticity. The model recorded none of the vowel features that marked Australian, New Zealand and Southern US speech, and gave /r/ to non-rhotic speakers in 73% of contexts, against the expert's 5%. Neither the anti-citation instruction nor a minimal prompt brought the transcription back to the speaker. A larger model, tested on 25 speakers, recorded more local features but also features the speakers did not produce. The article argues that standard language ideology enters the transcription through the reference the model applies to every speaker, and that AI transcriptions used in pronunciation teaching need to be checked by listening. Claude (Anthropic) and Consensus assisted with literature search, analysis scripts, revision and translation.

title: When Family Relationships Continue but Their Meaning Changes: The RENACER Model of Perceived Relational Meaning Asymmetry, Enduring Relational Grief, and Reconstruction of Belonging
abstract: Family relationships can change deeply even when family members continue living together, communicating, and participating in one another’s lives. When someone experiences broken trust, emotional hurt, or a lack of support, they may begin to see a family relationship differently. Yet other relatives may continue behaving as though nothing has changed, expecting the same closeness, loyalty, responsibilities, or trust as before. This difference can leave individuals feeling misunderstood, emotionally disconnected, and grieving a relationship that still exists. This article introduces RENACER, an integrative conceptual framework designed to explain how individuals experience and navigate changes in family relationships that are not fully recognized or acknowledged by others. RENACER identifies seven interconnected domains: Relational Expectations, Expectation Violation, Nonrecognition, Asymmetry in Relational Meaning, Cultural-Relational Reappraisal, Enduring Relational Grief, and Reconstruction of Self and Belonging. At the center of the framework is Perceived Relational Meaning Asymmetry (PRMA), which describes the experience of understanding a family relationship differently from how relatives continue to communicate, behave, and maintain expectations within that relationship. RENACER considers how multigenerational living arrangements, economic interdependence, caregiving responsibilities, and cultural commitments can make physical distancing difficult or undesirable. The framework challenges the assumption that personal autonomy and family loyalty are mutually exclusive, proposing that healthy individuation, self-respect, and boundaries can coexist with family connection and collectivist values. Drawing on social work, family science, and clinical psychology, RENACER offers theoretical propositions, testable hypotheses, implications for social work practice, and directions for future research on relational grief, identity, and belonging when family relationships continue but their meaning changes.

title: Measuring Immigrant Generations Across the Life Course: Evidence from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1979
abstract: Immigrant-generation comparisons underpin sociological accounts of incorporation, stratification and the life course, yet their validity depends on how longitudinal surveys record migration and family origins. We assess the U.S. National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1979 (NLSY79) as a resource for such research. Respondent and parental birthplace classified 12,041 of 12,686 participants (94.9%): 863 first-generation, 772 second-generation and 10,406 third-or-higher-generation respondents. Thirteen overlapping self-reported ancestry families were measurable for all first- and second-generation respondents; 12.3% and 23.3%, respectively, reported multiple families. First-entry timing was available for 71.4% of first-generation respondents and entry status for 70.2%. Classification loss varied by sex and historical racial/ethnic cohort, detailed public-use birthplace was unavailable and several intersectional cells were small. These findings show why immigrant generation, ancestry, arrival timing and racialised position should not be treated as interchangeable indicators. The NLSY79 supports broad generation comparisons and selected arrival-timing analyses, provided researchers disclose classification rules, denominators and subgroup constraints. The study offers an auditable measurement foundation for longitudinal sociology of migration and inequality.

title: Can a True Photograph Revive an Old Stereotype? Press Images, Representational Discrimination, and Iconographic Imprudence
abstract: This paper examines an authentic photograph selected and framed so as to stand for a broader political or moral reality. In April 2026, the cover of the Italian weekly L’Espresso concerning violence by Israeli settlers in the West Bank, sought to make a particular photograph emblematic of the occupation. The photograph is not alleged to be fabricated, nor does this paper dispute the reality of violence committed by some settlers. The question is whether it is consistent with the limits of ethical journalism to select, crop, title, and circulate an authentic image in such a way that visible markers of Jewish religious identity become part of the representation of culpability. This paper proposes one underlying condition, systemic epistemic weakness, and three related concepts arranged on a spectrum: (i) iconographic extension of culpability, (ii) iconographic imprudence, and, at the strong end, (iii) representational discrimination. It proposes seven factors for assessing editorial choices of this kind and tests them against the strongest objection, that the identity markers are pertinent and necessary to the story. This paper does not infer antisemitic intent on the part of L’Espresso, it does not claim to demonstrate actual audience effects, and it locates the case at the level of imprudence. It identifies a representational risk arising when a true individual case resonates with an older repertoire of false collective stereotypes. The paper concludes that editorial responsibility concerns not only whether an image is true, but also whether it is liable to create amalgams and thereby consolidate false accusations against religious groups.

title: U.S. Return Migration and Gendered Partnership Trajectories in Mexico
abstract: From 2010 to 2020, more people have left the United States for Mexico than vice versa, reversing a historical process that had lasted for over 50 years. Yet, return migrants remain understudied. In this paper, we use data from the 2017 and 2025 Survey of Retrospective Demographic Events to examine the sequences of partnership formation from ages 15 to 34 among U.S. return migrants and non-migrants in Mexico. We adopt a life course and gender perspective, given that the motivations, resources, and outcomes that define female and male migration are different. For men, migration reshapes the timing and stability of unions but it does not substantially interfere with union formation. Migrant men tend not to form unions while in the U.S., they postpone entering a union after return. They are also about twice as likely to experience a life course marked by separation compared to non-migrants. For women, migration is not associated with increased separation. Female return migrants are less likely to remain single and more likely to enter early cohabitation, a pattern consistent with family migration and social disadvantage. Our results shed light on the challenges of return migrants’ reintegration, in a context of increasingly restrictive U.S. immigration policies.

title: Intersectionality in health policy analysis: A scoping review
authors: Aaron Koay, Priscila de Morais Sato, Haoyue Guo, Sarah Dalglish, Arthur Davis, Sorcha Ní Chobhthaigh, Shao Yuan Chong, Edward Fottrell, Stephen Roberts, Audrey Prost
abstract: Introduction: Intersectionality is increasingly applied in health policy analysis, but its operationalisation has not been systematically examined. Methods: Following JBI guidance, this scoping review aimed to map the application of intersectionality in health policy analysis. Six bibliographic databases were systematically searched, supplemented by Google Scholar and backward citation searching. Two reviewers independently screened the retrieved records. Data were extracted using a bespoke theory-informed framework, examining six dimensions: conceptual clarity, analytical modality, categorical complexity, epistemic diversity, positionality and reflexivity, and transformative potential. Results: Of 131 included records, 78.6% were published from 2020 onwards. Among classifiable records, 81.4% of first authors were coded as women (105/129), and 78.7% were affiliated with institutions in high-income economies (100/127). Analyses were overwhelmingly retrospective (96.9%) and only 9.2% drew on theories of policy processes, governance, or political economy. Although 89.3% cited intersectionality scholarship, only 71.8% explicitly defined intersectionality and 20.6% applied a named intersectionality-informed policy analysis approach. Most records examined intersectional disadvantage without considering relative privilege (62.6%). Gender/sex was the axis most frequently selected a priori (80.0%) and most often given primacy. Reporting of participatory engagement (23.7%), positionality (33.6%), and deliberate reflexivity practices (8.4%) were uncommon. Most proposed policy or practice recommendations (88.5%), but only 29.3% of these explicitly called for liberation from oppression. Few reported challenges in applying intersectionality (9.2%) or proposed methodological improvements (6.9%). Conclusion: Overall, the adoption of intersectionality in health policy analysis has not been matched by consistent theoretical and methodological integration. Guidance is provided to support methodological application that is more theoretically grounded and oriented towards the redistribution of power and privilege.

title: Textual Reconstruction of Zo History
abstract: Chhînlung is not a literal cave nor a primordial homeland, but a mythologized memory of frontier enclosure and displacement experienced by Proto-Zo populations during the Nanzhao period, later resemanticized through Zo linguistic categories and oral tradition. Zo ethnogenesis is here understood as a gradual process unfolding within the Upper Chindwin–Kabaw frontier, shaped by political collapse, displacement, and sustained cultural contact rather than a single migration event. The paper first analyses the linguistics of Chhînlung, before triangulating evidence from Meitei chronicles, Arakan-Burmese traditions, and Chinese frontier documentation to deductively reconstruct Zo migration and ethnogenesis up to their movement into the Chin–Lushai Hills by the sixteenth century. Adopting a multidisciplinary framework, this study critically reconstructs early Zo history while situating it within the broader geopolitical and social dynamics of western Burma.

title: Mediating Revolution: Nonprofits, TED, & Silicon Valley
abstract: After the 2001 dot-com burst, TED became a 501(c)(3) nonprofit. Adopting such durably benevolent structure in the U.S. popular imagination, TED elucidates the nonprofit’s cultural work: disavowing economics alongside promised future change. Against hype’s cyclic crisis of value within promotional culture (Powers, 2012), the nonprofit’s interstitial and ambivalent structure aspires to fix and recuperate meaning against such crises. Through a textual analysis of decades of branding materials and taxes, I map TED’s structural arguments that entrench Silicon Valley’s democratic veneer, collapse elite networks to a public good, and naturalize platform capitalism. As techlash’s critique sees an increase of alternative, altruism-claiming organizations against the promise of structure-as-solution countering Big Tech and its authoritarian bent, looking back at TED’s example maps how organizational structure mediated revolution as intentional branding, a mode of futuring, and an (attempted) legitimation for such “democractic” futures that defined Silicon Valley to obscure its emergent broligarchic tendency.

title: Authentic-Content Misuse and AI-Related Content in Fact-Checked Misinformation from the 2026 Lebanon Conflict
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has intensified concern that synthetic media are reshaping misinformation during armed conflict, yet existing research on visual misinformation also shows that authentic images and video can mislead without any technical alteration, through recycling or false context. This study examines what forms of manipulation characterize fact-checked misinformation related to the 2026 Lebanon conflict between Israel and Hezbollah, with particular attention to the relative prominence of authentic-content misuse versus AI-related content. We conducted a descriptive computational analysis of 142 unique Arabic- and English-language fact-checked misinformation claims, applying a predefined manipulation-type taxonomy, an intra-rater repeat-coding reliability check, source-sensitivity analyses addressing the corpus's reliance on a single fact-checking organization, and a secondary analysis of whether claims penetrated professional news coverage. Authentic-content misuse accounted for 122 of 142 claims (85.9%), compared with 16 of 142 (11.3%) assigned to the AI-related primary group. Authentic-content misuse remained the majority in both sensitivity subsets restricting or removing the dominant fact-checking source (64.4% and 68.3%). Agreement between the original and repeat classifications on the grouped manipulation variable was 96.4% (Cohen's κ = 0.837). Under the study's documented search protocol, 2 of 142 claims (1.4%) were identified as having penetrated professional news coverage. Within this fact-checked corpus, authentic material used deceptively was substantially more common than AI-related content, suggesting that provenance and contextual verification remain important alongside synthetic-media detection. These findings describe one bounded, retrieval-dependent corpus and should not be read as an estimate of wartime misinformation generally.

title: Consumer Engagement through Predictive Intelligence and Automated Decision Systems: Examination of role of Artificial Intelligence in Modern Marketing
abstract: This working paper attempts to examine how machine learning, natural language processing and generative models are being embedded into marketing decisions. The examination moves the discipline from periodic, campaign-led planning toward continuous, evidence-based optimization. The study reviews the technological foundations of AI-enabled marketing, describes the data architecture that supports it. The working also proposes to analyses six major application areas for evaluation. These domains are recommendation and personalization, predictive scoring, programmatic advertising and attribution, conversational interfaces, generative content production, and dynamic pricing. Illustrative implementations from streaming, retail, beverages, beauty and business-to-business (B2B) software are discussed to show how these tools operate in practice. The paper also evaluates the risks that accompany adoption, including privacy exposure, embedded bias, model opacity, uneven access to capital and talent, and the temptation to manipulate rather than serve consumers. It concludes that durable advantage will not come from the sophistication of algorithms alone. It will come from organizations that pair automated decision systems with human judgment, treat customer data as a trust obligation, and measure success by long-term customer value rather than short-term click behaviour.

title: Digital Battlegrounds: Media, Behavior, and the Influence of Free Fire and Battlegrounds
authors: Santhosh Kumar S, Dr. Abdullah Alfazeena
abstract: The rapid proliferation of smartphones and high-speed internet in India has transformed digital gaming into a dominant leisure activity among youngsters. While gaming offers interactive entertainment, the excessive and uncontrolled use of specific mobile titles, notably Battlegrounds Mobile India (BGMI) and Garena Free Fire, has sparked significant concerns regarding digital game addiction. Moving away from traditional quantitative metrics and external qualitative observations, this study employs a rigorous autoethnographic methodology to deeply investigate the lived, internal experience of mobile game addiction. By utilizing self-generated data—including retrospective memory logs, reflective journal entries, and historical screen-time analysis—the researcher systematically documents their personal psychological trajectory from casual engagement to compulsive dependency. Grounded in the Uses and Gratifications Theory, the thematic analysis deconstructs how the sophisticated behavioral designs of these battle royale games, such as competitive rank-pushing, squad- based social dynamics, and continuous reward systems, hyper-efficiently satisfy fundamental psychological needs. The study illustrates how these virtual environments frequently act as a maladaptive coping mechanism to escape real-world academic pressures and insecurities. The self- analysis reveals that excessive immersion severely disrupts daily life, resulting in profound behavioral shifts including heightened irritability, verbal aggression, and extreme emotional volatility directly tied to in-game outcomes. Furthermore, the findings explicitly document significant academic displacement, physical and mental health consequences such as severe sleep disruption and underlying anxiety, and a tragic psychosocial substitution where real-world family bonds are neglected in favor of virtual squad loyalties. Ultimately, this autoethnographic research highlights that while digital games provide temporary escapism and a synthetic sense of status, uncontrolled addiction fundamentally destabilizes youth development. By documenting the visceral, real-world realities of mobile game addiction from the inside out, this study concludes by advocating for cognitive reframing, structured digital detoxification, and the active rebuilding of physical-world coping mechanisms to combat youth digital dependency.

title: Embodied Devotion and Ritual Performance: A Visual Ethnography of Veerapandi Gowmariamman Temple Festival, Theni
authors: Panneer Selvam. G, Dr. Abdullah Alfazeena
abstract: This study examines the embodied dimensions of ritual practices in the Veerapandi Gowmariamman Temple festival, Theni district, Tamil Nadu, through a visual-ethnographic approach grounded in embodiment theory. Moving beyond symbolic and textual interpretations of religion, the research focuses on how devotion is enacted through the body in rituals such as piercing, fire walking, river immersion, karagam carrying, and temple procession. Drawing on Thomas Csordas’s concept of embodiment, the study interprets the body as the primary site of religious experience, where meaning is produced through sensory engagement, physical endurance, and disciplined movement. Using photographic documentation as primary data, the study analyzes gesture, posture, spatial interaction, and collective participation to understand how ritual practices are lived and experienced. The findings reveal that the body functions as a sacred medium through which devotion is expressed, with pain, endurance, and multisensory immersion playing central roles in shaping spiritual experience. The study also highlights the importance of collective embodiment, where shared bodily participation reinforces social cohesion and cultural identity. Additionally, the interaction between the body and natural elements such as fire and water underscores the material and environmental dimensions of ritual practice. By situating ritual within the framework of embodiment theory, this study contributes to contemporary cultural and anthropological scholarship by demonstrating that religion is fundamentally a lived, corporeal experience. It further establishes the value of visual ethnography in capturing the non-verbal and performative aspects of ritual that are often overlooked in conventional research.

title: Cross-dialectal exposure effects on the production and perception of the French low-vowel contrast
authors: Scott Kunkel, Adam Chong, Esther de Leeuw
abstract: Individuals’ speech patterns can change after extended exposure to a second dialect (D2) of their native language, even in adulthood. While speech production changes in D2 acquisition are well documented, less is known about changes in perception and how production and perception interact. The present study investigates these issues in relation to geographically mobile speakers of Quebec French and Hexagonal French (the French of continental France) by comparing them to non-mobile speakers of each dialect. A sentence elicitation task and a two-alternative forced choice (2AFC) lexical identification task were used to assess change in production and categorical perception of /a ~ ɑ/, a phonemic contrast that is widespread in Quebec French yet largely merged to /a/ in Hexagonal French. Results revealed no effect overall of mobility on /a ~ ɑ/ realization in production, but an asymmetrical effect of mobility on perception among the mobile Hexagonal French participants. Additionally, a complex interplay was observed between changes to perception and production, challenging the notion of a direct link between these domains in D2 acquisition. These findings present evidence of post-adolescent, perceptual adaptation and suggest that such perceptual adaptation is not linearly associated with production-based changes in D2 acquisition.

title: Visualizing Neighborhood Racial Disparities in Flock’s Surveillance Network across the United States
abstract: A growing body of sociological work documents neighborhood disparities in state surveillance. This data visualization expands on this work by mapping uneven patterns in the locations of Flock automated license plate readers (ALPR). I draw on crowdsourced data on the locations of 116,309 Flock ALPR cameras to describe the characteristics of census block groups (CBG) by camera density. These data provide an unprecedented view into the national distribution of police surveillance infrastructure. More than a quarter of Americans live in a CBG with at least one Flock camera. Furthermore, CBGs with more cameras have larger shares of racially minoritized residents. This uneven pattern is strongest in rural areas and largely absent in cities. These findings suggest that racially minoritized residents, particularly those in rural areas, may face disproportionate exposure to this growing network of algorithmic surveillance.

title: The Male Abstraction Bias in Internet Culture and Large Language Models
abstract: Conceptual abstraction and gender are two equally central aspects of the human mind, yet they have traditionally been studied in isolation from one another, as though they were fundamentally separate. Here, we find gender and abstraction are systematically linked throughout the space of concepts spanning single (N = 40,000) and multi-word expressions (N = 67,000): across billions of words and millions of images on the internet --- and across numerous measurement techniques, including human and AI classifications --- more abstract concepts are more associated with men, a pattern we show replicates in languages around the world. This male abstraction bias not only holds across semantic domains, but it also maps onto grammatical structure: verbs and adverbs are more abstract and more male-coded, revealing a system-wide trace of stereotypes accentuating agentic qualities in men. Furthermore, we show this bias readily emerges in the free associations humans and AIs produce in controlled online tasks, indicating its psychological internalization and its algorithmic reproduction. These findings identify a latent structure in conceptual space that unifies a range of stereotypes: for example, framings of women as more embodied, emotional, and warm, versus men as more cognitive, rational, and competent; as well as erroneous views of men as better at mathematics, science, and engineering. More broadly, by analyzing an unprecedently large, multimodal sample of online data, we provide culture-wide evidence of gender as a core organizing principle shaping conceptual space far beyond the characterization of people and social roles.

title: The Political Reach of Non-Political TikTok Accounts
authors: Cristina Monzer, Silvia Téliz, Cameron Moy, Yuzhe Lei, Deen Freelon
abstract: Research on political expression online typically classifies accounts by partisan or ideological identity, an approach that works well when an account’s political expression signals its political leaning. On TikTok, accounts often address politics in ways that say little about their political identity. We therefore take political expression as our starting point, analyzing 2,116 high-visibility U.S. TikTok accounts and 104,191 of their videos. A latent class analysis of self-presentation, off-platform notability, and posting practices reveals five account types: Political Specialists, Value-based Creators, Prolific Celebrities, Lifestyle Creators, and Intermittent Celebrities. Partisan labels were rare in bios, and the identity markers accounts did display in their profiles focused most on their professional roles, content creation, and family and relationships. Political Specialists, the accounts organized around politics, posted the most political content, accounting for 29.1% of political videos in our sample but only 10.1% of their views. Prolific Celebrities and Lifestyle Creators received 86.2% of all views for political videos in our sample. On TikTok, political reach belongs less to political accounts than to those for which politics is occasional, and classifying accounts by political identity or institutional role would miss most of it.

title: Uncovering Hidden Populations: A Network-Based Approach to Estimate Child Trafficking Prevalence
authors: Dennis M. Feehan, Guy Grossman, Biz Herman, Maya Shuen Lu, Cecilia Hyunjung Mo
abstract: Measuring hidden populations, such as child trafficking victims, is difficult: victims are hard to reach and are often reluctant to disclose their experiences, so direct surveys understate prevalence. We evaluate network elicitation as an alternative, comparing estimates based on reports about close friends, about acquaintances, and self-reports. We field all three in a single nationally representative household survey of 1,474 Jamaican children aged 12 to 17, who report on themselves and on their networks, and we measure seven locally common forms of trafficking.
