Exploratory analyses suggested that the SES-word comprehension correlation strengthened with child age; and that touch-based measures led to smaller SES-word comprehension associations than both looking- and pointing-based measures. We discuss these findings to inform future empirical, theoretical, and applied research.

title: Disconnected Neighborhoods: Segregated Interactions and Cognitive Health in Middle-Aged and Older Adults
authors: Jiwon Jang, Dylan Connor, Connor Sheehan, Joseph Saenz
abstract: Residential segregation constrains interaction across social lines, operating as an established place-based risk factor for health. Yet, studies conventionally operationalize segregation through static residential composition rather than active patterns of interaction. This study examines segregation by capturing both residents’ characteristics and their movement through broader neighborhood networks, as inferred from collective travel patterns. We use the Spatial Preference in Local Interaction (SPLIT) index – a mobility-based, tract-level measure of cross-neighborhood segregation – and link it to American Community Survey data on tract-level prevalence of cognitive impairment among middle-aged and older adults from 2018 to 2023. We find that cognitive impairment is significantly lower in tracts where mobility networks are economically diverse yet racially and ethnically homogeneous – a pattern consistent with the protective effects of in-group cohesion (bonding) and cross-area resource acquisition (bridging). These findings suggest that the cognitive consequences of cross-neighborhood interaction resist simple characterization, underscoring how residential ties regulate access to both proximate community supports and wider economic opportunity structures.

title: Generalized Local Additive Spatial Smoothing (GLASS): A New Approach to Mitigating the Modifiable Areal Unit Problem in Local Regression Modeling
abstract: Addressing spatial non-stationarity and the Modifiable Areal Unit Problem (MAUP) in regression models is essential for accurate spatial analysis. This study extends the Generalized Local Additive Spatial Smoothing (GLASS) framework, a technique that leverages spatial smoothing to adjust the spatial support of covariates to a specified target within local modeling. By doing so, GLASS mitigates MAUP-related biases that arise from data aggregation that could distort the inference of local processes. Unlike traditional local regression approaches, which assume consistent spatial support across covariates and often require prior aggregation before model calibration, GLASS endogenously aligns differing supports during estimation. A multivariate extension is introduced that integrates adaptive smoothing and variable-specific bandwidth selection through a nested iterative backfitting procedure. Simulation experiments and an empirical case study modeling diabetes prevalence in the Washington D.C.– Maryland–Virginia region demonstrates that GLASS outperforms Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR) and Multiscale GWR, offering a promising framework for analysing spatially heterogeneous relationships across misaligned supports.

title: The Geography of Electioneering in Multi-Party Systems: Evidence from Campaign Poster Locations in Central Berlin
abstract: Election posters are an omnipresent yet understudied feature of election campaigns. While some researchers have studied poster design and its processing by voters in lab settings, the spatial dimension of poster placement — where parties place their posters and why — has received almost no systematic attention. This study examines the geography of electioneering in multi-party systems, drawing on a novel dataset of geolocated poster locations from Friedrichshain-Kreuzberg, a dense and politically diverse district of Berlin where evenly spread posters could reach most residents, making it a least-likely case for spatial targeting. By walking every street of the district and photographing all visible posters during the 2025 German federal election campaign, we assembled more than 6,800 geolocated photographs capturing over 10,000 individual posters, to our knowledge the most comprehensive dataset of its kind. We extract and classify every poster with a five-stage automated image-analysis pipeline that combines object detection (Florence-2, GroundingDINO), CLIP-based clustering into campaign motifs, and GPT-4o classification. Its output closely matches hand-coding and offers a reproducible and transferable way of measuring physical campaign material. Linking the full corpus of geolocated and classified posters to precinct-level electoral results from 2021, we show that mobilization is the primary logic of poster placement: Parties place their posters close to where they did well in the previous election. This is not to say that parties do not chase new voters at all; however, when they do, they fish in the pond of parties that belong to the same political bloc as they do and utilize their core issues (i.e., issues important to their electorates). These findings highlight the enduring strategic relevance of offline campaigning and call for greater attention to the geography of party competition.

title: Workplace-Based Interventions for Healthy Aging in the Transition to Retirement: A Scoping Review
abstract: Background: The transition from work to retirement offers a window of opportunity to promote healthy aging, and before labor market exit, the workplace reaches people through their employment. This review maps workplace-based prevention and health promotion interventions for healthy aging in this transition. Methods: This scoping review followed JBI methodology and PRISMA-ScR. Five databases and citation tracking were searched for studies published from January 2016 to July 2026. Interventions were characterized by transition phase, form of employer involvement, healthy aging domains, and definition of the target population, based on the World Health Organization framework of intrinsic capacity and functional ability. Results: Five studies from four countries were included. The employer provided access to participants for all five interventions, but only one intervention was fully workplace-embedded. Four interventions were delivered before the labor market exit, and only one, a peer mentoring program, was designed to continue across it. All interventions were multidomain and centered on psychosocial and mental health and social participation, but none addressed cognitive functioning. All studies defined their populations by proximity to the exit, yet none defined the transition, and only one timed its outcome measurements to the retirement date. Conclusion: Within a small evidence base that limits generalization, the interventions used the reach of the workplace almost exclusively before the exit, although this access ends with it. Prevention across the transition would need to separate access, delivery, and continuation. Research needs controlled studies that define the exit, extend across it, and address intrinsic capacity, including cognitive functioning. Systematic Review Registration: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/YN6TK

title: Land Reallocation and Climate Damages to Agriculture: Evidence from Brazil
abstract: How climate change affects agricultural output depends on how it shifts potential yields across crops and locations, and on how readily farmers move land among crops and into other uses. We estimate this response with a random-coefficients logit on Brazilian Agricultural Census data, in which plots value crops at world prices times their own FAO-GAEZ potential yields. Own-price crop area elasticities average about 1, and total cropland responds with an elasticity of 0.5 as land moves between crops and pasture. Under a high-emissions scenario (SSP3-7.0) for 2041--2060, climate change reshapes where crops are grown: crop area falls in today's breadbaskets but rises in two-fifths of regions, and this reallocation amplifies the output effects of yield changes. Nationally, farm income falls by 2.3% of crop revenue, yet regions holding three-quarters of Brazil's farmland lose twice that amount, and reallocation offsets a fifth of the damages.

title: Advancing Interpretive Mapping as a Co-Design Method for Post-Mining Transition: Conditional Reasoning, Development Sequencing, and Mutual Understanding
abstract: Mine closure extends beyond individual sites as a regional transition issue, with implications for community livelihoods and long-term wellbeing. Yet community input is often gathered separately from technical decision-making, limiting shared spatial negotiation around post-mining futures. Grounded in landscape urbanism, interpretive mapping has long been used to represent layered spatial knowledge. This study applies that capacity through an exploratory co-design workshop to examine how expert knowledge and community priorities can be brought together amid the staged coal phase-out in Australia’s Latrobe Valley. Through individual assessment, collective mapping, and discussion, participants prioritised three proposals that consolidated key concerns: wetland recovery, industrial heritage, and biodiversity rehabilitation. Within this process, participants positioned the proposals in specific locations and timeframes, while final reassessment showed that views on proposal value remained varied after negotiation. The study advances interpretive mapping beyond knowledge layering and visualisation, translating diverse knowledge and deliberation into shared judgement about post-mining futures. It also exposes a critical implementation gap: prioritised proposals are difficult to advance without governance clarity, technical feasibility, and funding pathways. The paper argues that accessible co-design must be embedded within an adaptive transition framework aligning rehabilitation decisions with regional development agendas, so design proposals can move toward staged delivery.

title: From Earth-Centric to Space-Centric Geopolitics: Rethinking Power Beyond the Planet
abstract: The rapid expansion of state and commercial activity in outer space is reshaping foundational assumptions about geopolitical power and international order. This article examines how emerging space practices, ranging from satellite warfare and resource extraction to planetary colonization, challenge Earth-centric frameworks that have long dominated international relations theory. Drawing on recent U.S. policy shifts and a critical case study of the 2025 Senate hearings for NASA Administrator nominee Jared Isaacman, the analysis identifies a key fault line between competing strategic divisions: NASA’s multilateral Artemis framework and SpaceX’s Mars-directed approach. To interpret these developments, the article proposes a typology of geopolitical perspectives, Earth-centric, Earth-bound, and space-centric, and argues that a space-centric lens offers a richer understanding of how outer space is becoming a source, not just a site, of political order. The findings suggest that expanding the conceptual boundaries of geopolitics is essential for understanding contemporary transformations in global power and institutional authority.

title: Applying the Technology Acceptance Model to Cloud Computing Adoption in Developing Countries: Lessons from Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises in Cameroon
abstract: The Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), developed by Davis in 1989, remains one of the most widely used frameworks for explaining technology adoption, yet it was developed in Western contexts and for the technologies of three decades ago. This paper reviews the literature on cloud computing features, service models (SaaS, PaaS, IaaS), and deployment models (private, public, hybrid, community), and on factors influencing cloud adoption in SMEs, and tests TAM's fit for Cameroon. Drawing on a qualitative grounded theory study of nine participants in three Cameroonian SMEs, the paper shows that perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use powerfully shaped adoption, while competitive pressure, organizational innovativeness, government policy, vendor trust, infrastructure, and security concerns, factors outside the original TAM, were also decisive. The paper argues for using TAM as a structuring guide extended with contextual constructs when studying cloud adoption in developing countries.

title: Analyzing the Impact of Cloud Computing in SMEs: A Study of Adoption, User Experience, and Performance in Cameroon (Doctoral dissertation)
abstract: Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) play an essential role in fostering innovation, productivity, job creation, and competitiveness at national and international levels. SMEs face unique challenges in accessing and utilizing cloud computing, a technology that offers critical resources for growth, but whose adoption in Cameroonian SMEs is notably lacking. This study examines the adoption, user experience, and impact of cloud computing on SMEs in Cameroon. Using a qualitative grounded theory approach grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the research seeks to understand the factors influencing low adoption rates despite apparent advantages, focusing on implications for organizational growth and competitive advantage. Data were collected from interviews with nine participants across three SMEs in Buea, Douala, and Yaounde. Findings reveal benefits such as enhanced competitiveness, increased customer satisfaction, cost savings, improved disaster recovery, strengthened data security, improved performance and reliability, and enhanced collaboration. However, obstacles including knowledge gaps, financial constraints, privacy and security concerns, poor internet access, and lack of adequate support remain significant. Recommendations are provided for SMEs, cloud providers, and policymakers to boost cloud integration into Cameroonian SMEs and to promote economic growth in developing countries, especially within Africa.

title: When Newspapers Block AI, Who Speaks to Voters? A Game-Theoretic Model of a Business Standoff with Political Externalities
abstract: Major newspapers block AI crawlers, while parties and partisan sites leave their text open. This paper builds a game-theoretic model of the hold-out and asks what voters hear while it lasts. In the model, an AI that cannot grade its sources pools the text it can read; two persuaders choose how much nearly free text to publish; and an AI lab may license a newspaper's reporting for its lost revenue. Neither the newspapers nor the lab has a political aim. Three results follow. First, the persuaders flood the AI, and the lab licenses each newspaper once a fixed share of the voters closest to it asks the AI, whatever the AI says. Second, newspapers whose voters dislike the AI's answers more hold out longer, and their voters hear the flood longer. Third, licensing bends the persuaders' contest by a small tilt from where the costs alone put it: patient persuaders tilt the AI's answers against the voters' average ideology, and impatient ones toward it. Business decisions with no political aim thus set how long each group hears the flood and which way the AI's answers tilt.

title: Multiple causal mechanisms link biodiversity conservation initiatives with human well-being
authors: Louise Glew, Daniel C. Miller, Michael B Mascia
abstract: Sustainability science and sustainable development policies increasingly recognize the contribution of biodiversity conservation to human well-being. However, understanding of the linkages between conservation and human well-being remains limited. Empirical evidence on the existence, magnitude and variation in causal pathways is fragmented, hampering decision-makers’ ability to design conservation interventions that also support human well-being. Here we present a conceptual framework that identifies five major pathways through which conservation interventions affect human well-being: 1) governance, 2) ideas and information, 3) conservation infrastructure, 4) ancillary opportunities, and 5) ecosystem services. These pathways may interact, creating novel synergies and trade-offs, scale-dependency, and distributive effects that shape an intervention’s social impact. Use of such a multi-causal framework can help avoid skewing policy decisions and investments toward any one pathway. Recognition of the diverse mechanisms linking conservation and human well-being allows scholars and practitioners to better assess the contribution of biodiversity conservation to global sustainability.

title: Climate-Nutrition Policy Coverage and Implementation Provisions in National Documents of 10 Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Paired Document Analysis
abstract: Background: Climate change and malnutrition share causes, and governments should tackle them together. Few studies ask whether national policy documents link the two or contain the provisions needed to act on that link. A policy with no budget, owner, deadline, or consequence is hard to deliver. This matters most in low- and middle-income countries. We aimed to describe how fully national climate and nutrition documents cover eight policy domains, test whether fuller coverage goes with more implementation provisions, and find which provisions are most often missing. Method: We analyzed 21 national documents (10 nutrition, 11 climate) from 10 countries in Africa, Asia, the Pacific, and Latin America. Two reviewers scored each country on a coverage index (eight domains, 0 to 3 each; maximum 24) and a readiness index (six provisions, present or absent; maximum 6). A third researcher settled disagreements. Analyses were exploratory. Results: Median coverage was 14.5 and readiness 3.5. Monitoring appeared in all 10 countries, but only one had an accountability provision. Five had a dedicated budget. Financing was the weakest domain (mean 1.0 of 3). The indices correlated closely (ρ = .99), partly because they share anchors. A version with less overlap gave ρ = .90 (95% CI .56 to 1.00), the safer estimate. Conclusion: Countries describe how they will track progress, yet almost none say who answers when targets are missed. Governments revising these plans should add accountability and financing provisions. These findings concern policy text, mostly second-round NDCs, not delivery, and need testing against implementation data and newer documents.

title: Traversal direction changes priorities in multiple criteria decision analysis
authors: Sajid Siraj, Barbara Summers, Simon Thomas van Baal, Valerie Belton
abstract: Hierarchical structuring is routine in multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA), and the direction in which decision-makers traverse the hierarchy is usually treated as a matter of analyst convenience. Weights can be elicited top-down, from broad objectives to their sub-criteria, or bottom-up, from the detailed criteria upwards. We test whether this choice really is inconsequential. In a within-participant experiment, 1,070 participants in three countries evaluated the same four alternatives under both approaches. We compare the approaches on the weights they produce and on how well their scores match participants' own informed preferences. Direction had a small effect on fit (d_z = -0.174): top-down scores were slightly closer, but bottom-up fitted better for 43% of participants. Direction had a large effect on the weights (d_z = +0.669): bottom-up elicitation moved weight towards the branches divided into more sub-criteria. Participants rated the two procedures as equally useful, intuitive, easy and enjoyable, yet chose the better-fitting one more often than chance. None of the psychological measures we collected predicted which approach suited a given person, and neither approach reproduced participants' informed top choice more than 40% of the time, against a 25% chance benchmark. Traversal direction therefore matters less for the decision reached than for the explanation of priorities that comes with it. Since the weights are what an MCDA study records, communicates and defends, we argue that they should be reported together with the hierarchy and elicitation level that produced them.

title: Psychological distress after ectopic pregnancy in adolescents: a narrative review of the evidence and UK support pathways
abstract: Ectopic pregnancy is an early pregnancy loss that can kill, and it arrives as four things at once: an emergency, a surgical or medical intervention, a bereavement, and a question about future fertility. Prospective cohorts recruited in UK early pregnancy units show that around one in five women meets the criteria for probable post-traumatic stress nine months afterwards, with anxiety and depression persisting in a substantial minority. Those cohorts excluded anybody under eighteen. Adolescents have therefore not been studied as a distinct group in this literature, and no adolescent-specific prevalence figure exists to be cited. What can be assembled instead is the adjacent evidence, and it points one way. Adolescent early pregnancy loss and adolescent pregnancy are both associated with grief, depressive symptoms, low self-esteem and suicidal thoughts, which suggests that teenagers are at least as vulnerable as adults and possibly more so. Psychosocial intervention reduces depression, anxiety and grief after perinatal loss, and structured support reduces distress in pregnant adolescents. So the problem is not that nothing works. In the UK, support after ectopic pregnancy rests on general practice follow-up, NHS counselling and the voluntary sector. For a young person, reaching any of it is shaped by confidentiality, waiting times and fragmented pathways. This review sets out what the evidence supports, what it cannot yet support, and four things that could be done now: routine psychological screening after ectopic pregnancy in young people, prompt age-appropriate follow-up, a defined route between early pregnancy services and adolescent mental health care, and prospective UK studies of the group nobody has measured.

title: Buying Against the Panic: The 1912 Russian Banking Syndicate and the Limits of Price Intervention
abstract: The Russian banking syndicate of 1912 was designed to defend eight industrial shares during the Balkan crisis with State Bank credit, fixed purchase prices and security-specific quotas worth 16.845 million rubles at the protocol prices. We link the protocol and purchase ledgers to daily exchange quotations and 11,677 trades by margin clients. The eight supported shares had been selected after unusually severe September losses: between 17 and 29 September they lagged the other regularly quoted shares by 5.9 log percentage points, a gap matched by only 0.7% of random sets of eight shares. Trend-free difference-in-differences estimates show no lasting post-intervention advantage. Cumulated through year-end, the estimates are −4.2 percentage points (95% CI −17.2 to 8.7) relative to the rest of the market and +3.2 points (−10.9 to 17.3) within sectors, excluding a large gain above about 17 points while leaving moderate effects possible. Comparative interrupted time-series estimates are larger because they extrapolate the September dip. Event studies of purchases recorded by the Russo-Asiatic Bank show no positive abnormal returns after either state-sponsored or private syndicate purchases. Transaction quotations remained near the prescribed purchase prices mainly for shares with larger quotas. By 2 October, the Russo-Asiatic Bank had bought 11,445 Putilov shares, equivalent to 95.4% of the 12,000-share quota specified in the protocol of 4 October. Margin clients did not shift their purchases toward the supported shares. The evidence therefore supports a narrow conclusion: visible, stock-specific purchase limits could absorb selling temporarily but did not leave a durable relative-price effect.

title: An educational paper on how to co-produce mental health research: Reflections and recommendations from people with lived experience of mental illnesses
authors: Lindsay Dewa, Jan Davies, Jan Speechley, Jane Taylor., Michael McTernan, Louise Ting, Tate Kambeu, Anna Lawrence-Jones, Richard Morley, Olufisayo Elugbadebo
abstract: Co-produced mental health research is scarce but increasingly conducted. Efforts to develop best practice guidelines are improving too. We aimed to write an educational paper with practical recommendations for researchers who are new to co-producing mental health research. We brought together a diverse team of authors with expertise and extensive experience in using principles of co-production in various stages of mental health research. Within the team, we reflected on, discussed and agreed on key considerations, challenges and recommendations for other researchers to take forward in their research. We describe several examples of how to co-produce mental health research using a set of co-production principles across the research cycle. We agreed that building relationships and sharing power in research with people with lived and/or living experience of mental illnesses can be difficult. This is because of complex factors including deep-rooted systemic issues, e.g. social and economic factors, and inequality perceptions, safeguarding considerations (e.g. emotional distress) and clinician/researcher difficulty in balancing power and safety. Dedicating sufficient time, effort, and resources for everyone to feel safe and breaking down pre-existing barriers to co-producing mental health research is crucial. Individual safeguarding and wellbeing plans for all are recommended. While co-producing mental health research is challenging, it is rewarding and worthwhile. The recommendations in this paper on applying co-production principles across research stages can help others co-produce mental health research. In particular, it offers more examples from qualitative studies and systematic reviews.

title: Women's Leadership in the Office of Religious Affairs: Meritocracy and Gender Equality Perspectives
abstract: The appointment of women as Heads of the Office of Religious Affairs (KUA) in 2026 marks a crucial milestone in the history of Indonesia's religious bureaucracy. This event not only reflects the expansion of women's access to strategic positions within the Ministry of Religious Affairs but also demonstrates the implementation of meritocratic principles in public office recruitment. This article aims to analyze the appointment of women as KUA Heads through the lenses of meritocracy and gender equality, as well as to examine its implications for the transformation of religious services. This study employs a normative legal research method, utilizing both conceptual and statute approaches. Data sources are drawn from statutory regulations, policy documents from the Ministry of Religious Affairs, and scholarly literature on the merit system, representative bureaucracy, and gender equality. The findings indicate that the appointment of women as KUA Heads is a logical consequence of bureaucratic reform that prioritizes competence, integrity, and performance as the baseline for career promotion. Furthermore, this policy strengthens female representation within the religious bureaucracy and holds the potential to enhance the quality of public services, making them more inclusive, responsive, and adaptive to community needs. These findings confirm that meritocracy and gender equality are not conflicting concepts; rather, they operate synergistically to support the transformation of a professional, public-service-oriented religious bureaucracy.

title: From Oil Shock to Domestic Inflation: Exchange-Rate Transmission of a Strait of Hormuz Disruption in the Democratic Republic of the Congo
authors: Christian P. Pinshi, Kevin M. Ngunza, Schadrack D. Kumenga
abstract: This paper examines the transmission of oil-price shocks to inflation in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), using the 2026 disruption of the Strait of Hormuz as the motivating geopolitical episode. Using 62 weekly observations from January 2025 to March 2026, we estimate a short-run autoregressive distributed-lag model, ADL(2,1,2), with Newey–West heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent standard errors. The results show substantial but dynamically stable inflation persistence. Brent-price increases have a positive but modest and transitory direct effect: a US$10-per-barrel increase raises weekly inflation by about 0.09 percentage point on impact, but the cumulative effect declines to about 0.04 percentage point. Exchange-rate variations exert a stronger and more persistent effect: a 1 percent depreciation of the Congolese franc against the US dollar is associated with a cumulative increase of about 0.22 percentage point. These findings identify the exchange rate as the main observable amplification channel for external price shocks in the highly dollarized Congolese economy. The results suggest that the analysis of energy shocks in dollarized economies should give particular attention to second-round effects, exchange-rate dynamics and inflation expectations.

title: From environmental data to equitable action: E-PHIA, an equity-centred framework for AI-enabled public health intelligence
abstract: Environmental health inequalities arise from interactions among environmental hazards, social disadvantage, population susceptibility and unequal capacity to respond. Public-health systems increasingly generate environmental, demographic, geospatial and health data, yet these information streams are often fragmented across surveillance and decision-making systems. Geospatial artificial intelligence (GeoAI) creates opportunities to integrate complex spatial data and identify patterns of environmental and population-health risk, but technical capability alone does not ensure equitable or actionable public-health decision-making. This conceptual paper proposes E-PHIA (Equity-Centred Public Health Intelligence with AI), an evidence-informed framework for translating environmental, population-health and social-vulnerability data through responsible AI and GeoAI into geographically actionable intelligence. E-PHIA comprises six connected layers: environmental intelligence; population-health and social-vulnerability intelligence; data integration and quality; responsible AI/GeoAI; actionable public-health intelligence; and action, evaluation and learning. Equity, explainability, fairness, privacy, governance and human oversight operate as cross-cutting safeguards. The framework introduces Equity Checkpoints across the intelligence lifecycle and distinguishes model performance from decision performance and population impact. It also proposes a conceptual prioritisation function in which public-health priority depends on hazard, exposure, vulnerability and actionability rather than environmental exposure alone. E-PHIA positions AI as an augmentation of professional public-health judgement, not a substitute for it. Empirical work is required to test data feasibility, technical and spatial validity, subgroup fairness, decision utility and population impact. The framework offers a testable pathway for moving from fragmented environmental data and retrospective reporting towards earlier risk identification, geographically targeted prevention and continuous evaluation of whether public-health action narrows or widens inequalities. Keywords: artificial intelligence; GeoAI; environmental health; public health intelligence; health inequalities; health equity; environmental epidemiology; public health surveillance; responsible AI; climate health

title: Companion AI and Psychological Health: Resource or Risk? Affective Design as the Mechanism of the Human–Machine Bond
abstract: This article examines, through a critical and integrative review of the literature (2024–2026), the extent to which affective bonds with companion artificial intelligences constitute a resource or a risk for psychological health, considering attachment, loneliness, well-being, and identity, and how the affective design of these systems produces such effects. The analysis indicates that the human–machine bond is a predictable effect of an affective engineering that simulates reciprocity and continuity (intimacy by design; designed relationality), rather than an error or deficit on the part of the user. Its effects, however, are neither intrinsically beneficial nor harmful: they act as an amplifier of the user’s prior psychological trajectory (AI Amplifier Effect), modulated by self-regulation, peer community, and sociocultural context. It is concluded that the bond is real yet asymmetric and functional, and that clinical and ethical evaluation should shift from the question of whether AI replaces the human bond to the question of what kind of bond affective design produces, in whom, and under what conditions—regulating the design rather than pathologizing the user.

title: Government Intervention in Communal Conflict Management in Edo State, Nigeria: Reported Strategies, Perceived Effectiveness and Institutional Constraints
abstract: Background: Communal conflict continues to challenge public authority and social cohesion in Nigeria. Government responses may contain immediate violence, yet durable peace also depends on how disputed claims are managed, institutions coordinate and affected communities participate. Objective: This study examines respondents’ reports of conflict triggers, government intervention strategies, perceived effectiveness and implementation constraints in five conflict-affected local government areas (LGAs) in Edo State, Nigeria. Methods: The study used a descriptive cross-sectional survey. A structured questionnaire was administered to 150 respondents drawn through stratified random sampling from Ministry of Interior officials, community leaders and residents in conflict-prone areas. The reported analysis uses frequencies and percentages, including responses to five-point Likert items. Findings: Land and boundary disputes were the most frequently reported conflict trigger (62%), while deployment of security personnel was the most visible intervention (57%). Forty-eight per cent agreed or strongly agreed that interventions reduced recurrence; 36% were neutral. Fifty-nine per cent reported that conflict recurred within 12–24 months following intervention. Inadequate funding (68%), overlapping authority with state agencies (55%) and limited perceived community involvement were prominent concerns. Conclusion and implications: The results indicate a perceived gap between visible crisis response and sustained, participatory conflict management. Since the study is descriptive and based on respondents’ accounts, the findings should be interpreted as perceptions rather than causal estimates or independently verified conflict rates. Recommendations focus on coordination, fair dispute settlement, community-linked early warning, operational resourcing and post-conflict follow-up.

title: Diaspora Diplomacy or Digital Mobilization? Voices from Abroad, Platforms and Generative AI in the Gen Z Protest Wave, 2024-2026.
abstract: Youth-led protests between 2024 and 2026 drew in people outside their countries: exiled commentators, migrant workers, students abroad and settled diasporas. Was this diaspora diplomacy, or digital mobilization of audiences at home? Coding 40 cross-border actions, grouped into 24 campaigns, documented in English, French and Bangla sources across six episodes centered on Bangladesh, I find that action from abroad was aimed mostly at home, although the share depends on how it is counted. Diaspora diplomacy appeared once institution-facing sources were searched, but rarely on behalf of the movements themselves. The article’s main contribution concerns voice. Building on representative-claims theory, I define self-appointed representation from abroad and separate representative claims, directives and boundary-drawing, mandates, and four kinds of uptake. In Bangladesh after the uprising, two exiled commentators issued directives and drew the uprising’s boundaries without any mandate; crowds sometimes acted in sequence with their posts, and others pushed back. The cases suggest that platforms let visibility become representative authority without organizational accountability, and that generative AI cheapens counterfeit claims about hidden backers.

title: How and Under What Conditions Does Data Analytics Improve Managerial Decision-Making?
abstract: Data analytics is widely used to support managerial decisions, but it is not clear how, and under what conditions, it improves them. This systematic literature review examines how data analytics affects managerial decision-making, through which mechanisms, under which conditions, and whether the picture differs between operational and strategic decisions. The review follows the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Searches in Google Scholar in October 2026, limited to 2015 to 2026, retrieved 391 records. After duplicates were removed, 365 records were screened, and together with four records from other methods, 205 were assessed for eligibility. Thirty-nine studies were included. The abstract was read for 22 of them and only the title and text snippet were available for the other 17, so the findings describe the evidence base and not each study in full. Most studies are cross-sectional surveys. Decision quality is the outcome studied most often, and analytics is usually linked to better decision outcomes. The effect works mainly through knowledge sharing, information processing, organizational capabilities and culture, and the speed and thoroughness of the decision process. It depends on analytics skills, data quality, governance, culture, firm size and the situation, and better decisions do not always lead to better organizational results. No included study compares operational and strategic decisions, so that question remains open. The review offers a conceptual framework and five propositions for future research, and it calls for stronger research designs, independent measures of decision quality and direct comparisons of decision levels. Keywords: data analytics; managerial decision-making; decision quality; analytics capability; systematic literature review

title: The Contingency System: A Synthetic Reconstruction of the Contingency Paradigm
abstract: Social theory in recent decades has been dominated by the idea of contingency, yet its content remains fragmented among communicative, relational, realist, ideational, and operational versions. This article reconstructs them into an overarching framework of a contingency system composed of four logically linked contingencies, each equipped with its own heuristic instrument: single (phenomenological), double (epistemic), triple (discursive), and fourth (ideological with epistemological argumentation). The epistemological procedure of the fourth contingency connects social alternatives with objective necessity and periodically revises the remaining three within an autopoietically developing social consciousness aimed at progress or the compensatory reconstruction of social relations toward beauty, humaneness, rationality, and truth. Social life thus proves to be simultaneously conditionally necessary and heuristically contingent. The framework offers a testable criterion for distinguishing between control and power: the maintenance versus the suppression of heuristic deliberation.

title: Systemic Tensions Around Water Territorialities for UNDROP Communities
abstract: The analysis of water resource access and management policies reveals a structural paradox: an increasingly regulatory, which contrasts with the reality of implementation.
